en: Now begins the seventh chapter.
I shall proclaim the duties of kings, how a monarch should conduct himself, how his origin comes about, and how he may attain supreme success.

It has been stated that the word *dharma* denotes what ought to be done (*kartavyatā*). The formal proposition here is that what must be performed by the king is now being declared. That which is to be done includes both that which has a visible purpose, such as the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) and so forth, and that which has an invisible purpose, such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice and so forth. In this context, however, that which has a visible purpose is primarily taught; for it is precisely therein that the established tradition of the king's duties (*rājadharmaprasiddhi*) resides.

The word *rāja* here does not denote the Kṣatriya caste; rather, it refers to a person endowed with qualities such as consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and sovereignty (*ādhipatya*). Therefore, he says: "As the king should conduct himself. By the mention of "king," he indicates the authority of one who possesses dominion over a realm (*janapada*). For the duties (*dharma*) mentioned here are based on other sources of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and not all are rooted in the Veda. And since they have other sources, only that which is not in conflict with the *Dharmaśāstra* is stated here. Thus, Kātyāyana says:
"Having set aside what is declared in the *Arthaśāstra*, one should follow what is declared in the *Dharmaśāstra*."

*Yathāvṛttaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose conduct (*vṛtta*) is such-and-such" or "one whose manner of being (*prakāra*) is such-and-such. The referent of the other member of the compound (*anyapadārtha*) is the king. If the primary emphasis were on the object itself (*yathārtha*), it would be an *avyayībhāva* compound. "Conduct" (*vṛtta*) refers to activity for the purpose of protection and for the sake of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). Its "origin" (*saṃbhava*) is its production, which has been described [in the preceding verses] beginning with, "The Lord created the King" (MDh 7.3). "Supreme success" (*paramā siddhiḥ*) is the sole sovereignty of one who desires victory. This is the promise of the fruit resulting from the king's conduct. (7.1)
By a Kṣatriya who has duly received the Brāhmaṇical consecration, the protection of all this [world] must be performed according to the law. (7.2)

"Brahma" refers to the Veda. The refinement (*saṃskāra*) prescribed therein is "Brahmic. This means that the refinement produced by the study of the Veda—which consists of both the mastery of the text and its comprehension of meaning—is brought to completion by the injunction for private recitation (*svādhyāya-vidhi*). It is logical, however, to call the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) "Brahmic," because its purpose is the acquisition of the Veda. As he will state later: "From those learned in the three Vedas, [he shall learn] the triple knowledge" (MDh 7.43). Otherwise, there would be the teaching of one who has already known what is to be known. The phrase "forty-eight refinements" refers to those beginning with conception (*garbhādāna*) and so forth, according to the Smṛti scriptures. By the words "by a Kṣatriya," it is indicated that only a Kṣatriya is entitled to sovereignty. Even in the absence of a Kṣatriya, the extension of these duties to others should be understood; otherwise, there would be the destruction of subjects—this is the intended sense. "For all" refers to those who pay taxes, as well as the poor and the helpless. The word "his" (*asya*) indicates the inhabitants of his own territory, specifying their respective districts and cities. "According to justice" (*yathānyāyam*): "justice" (*nyāya*) here means the scripture in the form of Dharmaśāstra, not the Arthaśāstra composed by Uśanas and others; it means without transgressing that. "Protection" (*parirakṣaṇa*) means preservation. It consists of warding off calamities, preventing the weak from being overwhelmed by the strong, and ensuring no one transgresses the boundaries of the scriptures. Protection is the shielding from suffering. Transgression of the scriptures leads to invisible suffering (in the afterlife); therefore, by not transgressing them, people become protected through fear of the king. If it is argued that royal punishment is suffering, [the reply is: royal punishment is minor compared to the great suffering of hell and other such realms. "It must be done" is the injunction. The qualification for this duty has been established in the eighth chapter. (7.2)
For when this world was without a king and everyone fled in every direction out of fear, the Lord created a king for the protection of all this. (7.3)
Whether he has fled, been oppressed, or is without support, he is the Lord, the Prajāpati. This is a hymn of praise. 7.3.
Having extracted the eternal portions from Indra, Anila, Yama, and Ārka; from Agni and Varuṇa; and from Candra and Vitteśa— 7.4.
Anila is the wind; Vitteśa is the lord of wealth, Vaiśravaṇa; mātrās are the constituent parts; śāśvatīḥ means those that are essential; nirhṛtya means having extracted. || 7.4 ||
Since the king was fashioned from portions of these lords of the gods,
he therefore overcomes all beings with his splendor.

Because he was fashioned from the portions (*mātrā*)—that is, the particles of splendor (*tejas*)—of these foremost gods, Indra and the rest, for that reason he overcomes others; his face becomes difficult to behold. This is due to the cause of his splendor. He was "extracted and fashioned," meaning produced; for the verbal root *kṛṣ* functions in the sense of "producing. Therefore, because it has the state of being the limit (*avadhi*) of the extraction, the word *mātrābhyaḥ* should be read either in the ablative or the instrumental case. (7.5)
Like the sun, he scorches both eyes and minds;
no one on earth is able even to look upon him. (7.6)

"He shines as if burning. He is described thus because he cannot be looked upon face-to-face. As it is said: "And one is not able to look at him on earth. Even Brāhmaṇas, who are superior by birth and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*), are unable to gaze directly at him. Thus it has been stated: "They should sit below while he is seated above" (GDh 11.7). 7.6.
By his own power, he becomes fire and wind; he is the sun, the moon, and the King of Dharma; he is Kubera, Varuṇa, and Indra. (7.7)

Because the deities beginning with Agni are the locus of the [five] measures (mātrā), they are described in this way by virtue of their connection to those powers. "Power" (prabhāva) refers to that which is a supramundane capacity. 7.7.
A ruler of the earth must not be despised even if he is a child, thinking "he is merely a human being";
for he is a great deity dwelling in the form of a man. (7.8)

Even a foolish king should not despise [another] thinking, "This is merely a human being. Rather, one should consider: "This is some great deity abiding here in human form. Therefore, it is improper to show contempt toward a king, even if no fault has been perceived. (7.8)
Fire burns only the man who approaches it carelessly;
but the fire of a king consumes the entire family, along with its livestock and accumulated wealth.

These are explanatory verses (*arthavāda*) regarding this rule. Although it concerns the duty of a king, it applies to all human goals. A man who touches fire with his hand or the like, or who stands too close even to a blazing fire, is a person who approaches it improperly; if he stumbles through negligence, he is burned. But a king, when enraged, consumes [the offender] along with his sons, wealth, wife, and kinsmen—whosoever they may be, including family members and relatives. Because of their connection to the offense, he destroys them together with their livestock and stores of wealth. (7.9)
Having truly considered the task at hand, as well as his own power, place, and time,
he repeatedly assumes various forms for the sake of accomplishing dharma.
One should not think, "The king is my kinsman" or "the king is my friend.
Whose friend could a king be, and who are the friends of a king?

Depending on their purpose, they behave toward an enemy as if toward a friend, and toward a friend as if toward an enemy. Likewise, being powerless, they tolerate some offense, but having gained power, they uproot it. The same applies to place and time. Therefore, for the sake of accomplishing dharma and for the sake of accomplishing his own ends, he assumes all forms. In one moment he is a friend, in another moment an enemy; a king is not of a single fixed nature. For this reason, one must not place trust in a king. One should not behave toward him with friendship, affection, or kindness, nor by regarding him as an equal in age or status; rather, he should always be regarded through the lens of political prudence (*naya*). (7.10)
In whose favor dwells the lotus-goddess Śrī, in whose prowess lies victory,
and in whose anger resides death— he indeed is composed of all splendor.

When pleased, he bestows prosperity through his propitiation; when angry, he joins one with death. Therefore, he should be propitiated by one who desires prosperity. Not only does he endow one with prosperity, but when satisfied, he slays even those enemies one possesses by overcoming them. Therefore, he should be served properly by one who desires the destruction of enemies.

Padmā: The word *padmā*, though a synonym for *śrī* (fortune), is employed here to signify greatness; the meaning is that she bestows great fortune. And these benefits are obtained by the king, because he, consisting of all splendor, bears the radiance of fire, the sun, and the moon. (7.11)
But he who hates him out of delusion will undoubtedly perish;
for the king sets his mind upon his swift destruction. (7.12)

People do not perish through the fear of transgression (*pratyavāya*) as they do out of greed for desired objects; therefore, he says again and again: "He who hates that king or acts with hostility toward him, he undoubtedly perishes. For his destruction comes quickly. Another person might tolerate an offense by reporting it to a king who is unable to act; in such a case, there may be a loss of wealth due to legal proceedings, and even a fact that has occurred may be altered due to the varying dispositions of witnesses—anticipating this, someone might even forgive [the offense]. However, when the king, with the intent to destroy that offender, keeps the offense in mind, he is surely afflicted [by the offender's power]; because the king possesses power, a conflict with one who is independent arises for him even as he exerts himself. (7.12)
Therefore, that lord of men should determine what is right for those he holds dear; and he should not deviate from that dharma even regarding those who are not dear. (7.13)

Since the king embodies all splendor (*tejas*), for that reason, he should determine and establish—having resolved—the law, that is, the settlement of affairs, among those who are dear and beloved, such as ministers and domestic priests, according to the requirements of the task, provided it is not contrary to the scriptures or established custom; he should not deviate from it. That kind of royal decree must not be transgressed—for example: "Today, a festival must be celebrated by everyone in the city; a wedding is taking place at the minister’s house, and everyone must assemble there. Likewise, no animals are to be slaughtered by the soldiers today; birds are not to be captured; and dancers are to be gratified by the wealthy for these many days. Similarly, even regarding undesirable persons: "No association with this person is to be made; entry into his house is not to be granted. Such a form of law, proclaimed by the king through the sounding of drums and other means, is not to be transgressed. However, the king does not have authority over the establishment of the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*) regarding the *agnihotra* and other rites, because that would lead to a contradiction with other *smṛtis*; and since there is no conflict in this specific matter, the statement is meaningful. (7.13)
For that purpose, the Lord formerly created Dharma, his own son, the protector of all beings, the staff consisting of the splendor of Brahman.

The origin of the king has been described. Now the origin of the rod of punishment is being stated. For him—that is, for the sake of that [king], and for the accomplishment of the king's purpose, the Lord Prajāpati created the rod of punishment.
What is the king's purpose served by the rod?

It is said: [He created] the protector of all beings. The "protector" is the guardian, and that is indeed the *daṇḍa* (the rod of punishment). Without the *daṇḍa*, a king is not able to protect. Therefore, the *daṇḍa* was created solely for the sake of establishing kingship. The phrase "Dharma, born of the Self, consisting of Brahman-splendor" is a praise of the *daṇḍa*. Dharma is not merely sacrifice, giving, and so forth; rather, it is the *daṇḍa* itself. Nor should this be understood as unrighteous (*adharma*) because it takes away life and wealth; on the contrary, this alone is Dharma. "Born of the Self" means he was born directly from the body of Prajāpati. He is not composed of the five elements; rather, he was fashioned from that which is the pure splendor (*tejas*) of Brahman. This was prior to the creation of the king. (7.14)
Out of fear of him, all beings, both stationary and moving, provide for his enjoyment and do not deviate from their own duties.

Out of fear of that punishment (*daṇḍa*), when only the relationship [of the punishment to the beings] is intended, there is no causality of fear; thus, the genitive case is used. Out of fear of punishment, stationary beings (*sthāvara*) become fit for enjoyment—that is, they become capable of providing enjoyment through fruits, flowers, shade, and so forth. For indeed, a stationary being that does not yield fruit is withered away. If it does not wither, because its location is pervaded on all sides, it is cut down and made into firewood. By this analogy of the tree, such should be done to the person who is subject to punishment—the one who acts against the King’s interests—and punishment should be administered by means of cutting, uprooting, and so forth. The mention of "stationary" beings is for the sake of praise as an illustration: such is this punishment that even stationary things are punished, how much more so mobile ones? However, stationary beings do not possess the notion that "this is my punishment. They do not deviate from their own nature; they do not flower out of season, nor do they bear fruit. (7.15)
Having truly considered the place, the time, the power, and the learning [of those involved],
he should appropriately apply [punishment] toward men who act unjustly.

This punishment is prescribed for those high ministers and others who act unjustly and commit acts detrimental to the king. However, regarding other litigants engaged in mutual disputes, it is stated [in MDh 8.126]: "Having fully ascertained the consequences (*anubandha*). This very verse has been explained in that same context. "Knowledge" (*vidyā*) here is superior, and its subject matter is the meaning of the Vedas. "As is fitting" (*yathārhatas*) means according to what is appropriate for each individual. "He should administer" (*saṃpraṇayet*) means he should set it in motion or carry it out. Having considered and examined all this, the punishment must be applied according to the specific circumstances of each case. If administered otherwise, it would bring visible harm to the king. The distinction between the seventh and eighth verses concerning the "Matrix of Punishments" (*daṇḍamātṛkā*) lies in the division between visible and invisible [consequences], and between one's own subjects and the people of the realm. 7.16
That king is the personification of punishment; he is the leader and the ruler, and he is remembered as the guarantor of the dharma of the four stages of life.

In reality, he alone is the king; for as long as he exists, there is royal power. He alone is the man who, by subduing even the most powerful men like women, brings them under his control. He is the leader, for by him all affairs are led. He is the ruler. "Ruling" (*śāsana*) is the king’s command; the state of being ruled depends upon punishment. His agency in accordance with *dharma* is merely figurative. Regarding the *dharma* of the four stages of life (*āśrama*), he stands like a guarantor (*pratibhū*); just as a guarantor does not permit deviation, so too does punishment. (7.17)
The rod governs all subjects; the rod alone protects them.
The rod remains awake while others sleep; the wise know the rod to be Dharma. (7.18)

The king does not govern through the treatises regarding what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, nor through injunctions and prohibitions; rather, it is punishment alone that does so. Punishment alone protects the weak from the powerful. Even when the king’s officers are asleep, it is only out of fear of punishment that the world does not behave according to its own whims. Punishment is of two kinds: royal punishment and the punishment of Yama. (7.18)
When properly supported through careful deliberation, he delights all his subjects;
but when implemented without due consideration, he brings about destruction on every side. (7.19)

It is maintained, refined, and set in motion. "Having considered" means having taken into account the previously mentioned factors such as place and time. It "delights," meaning it generates affection among the subjects. If applied in a contrary manner, not only does it fail to accomplish its own purpose, but being misapplied, it destroys the welfare of the people like poison. (7.19)
If the king did not tirelessly administer punishment to those deserving of it, the stronger would roast the weaker like fish on a spit. (7.20)

If punishment were not administered, those who are stronger—superior in strength, possessing greater physical power, having men with weapons in their hands, or being more numerous—would devour the weak like fish on a spit. Just as fish are impaled on spits for the sake of food, so too would a powerless person be preyed upon by those of superior power through the seizure of his wealth, body, wife, and so forth. Therefore, one should punish those deserving of punishment without negligence or laziness. One should not entertain the thought: "How can I possibly conduct an investigation? I shall simply not administer punishment. (7.20)

A crow might eat the sacrificial cake, and a dog might lick the oblation; there would be no sense of ownership in anything, and the social order would be overturned, with the low rising above the high. (7.21)

Even dogs, crows, and other such most base creatures would vie with the gods; they would consume the sacrificial offerings—such as the *caru* and *puroḍāśa* cakes—which ought to be given to the gods, were it not for their being restrained by punishment. Furthermore, that which constitutes ownership—the relationship between owner and owned—would cease to exist, as would the relationship between husband and wife or father and son. The husband would no longer be the master of his wife, and women would act according to their own will. There would be an inversion of high and low: that which is low, such as the *vṛṣala* (the Śūdra), would become superior and preeminent, while that which is superior, such as the Brāhmaṇa, would descend to inferiority. Śūdras would teach the Dharma, and Vedic Dharma would not be practiced. (7.21)
The whole world is kept in check by punishment, for a pure man is hard to find;
indeed, out of fear of punishment, the entire world is fit for the enjoyment of life. (7.22)

One who is pure and clean by very nature and by very essence regarding virtue, wealth, and pleasure—such a man is difficult to find; he can only be obtained through great hardships. However, one who is conquered by the rod is subdued by the rod and established on the right path; thus, he does not act according to his own whims. It has already been stated [previously] that this is for the enjoyment of the world (MDh 7.15). 7.22.
Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, birds, and serpents—even they are made to serve for the enjoyment [of others] when oppressed by punishment alone. (7.23)

The gods—such as Parjanya, Vāyu, Āditya, and so forth—are employed for the sake of enjoyment; they ripen the plants through their regulated cold, heat, and rain, out of fear and apprehension of His punishment. Otherwise, why would the sun and moon, or Dhātṛ and Parjanya, not deviate from their own fixed times of activity? If they possessed independence, perhaps the sun might not rise for two or three days at a time. But fearing punishment, he does not overstep his bounds. Thus says the Śruti: "Out of fear the sun shines; out of fear the moon gives heat."
"Out of fear of [the rod], both fire and wind [do not burn or blow excessively]" (KaṭhU 6.3).

That the Dānavas and others do not destroy this entire world day and night is due to the majesty of the rod. That moths, birds, and household ornaments such as parrots and mynas do not pluck out the eyes of children, and that hawks, crows, kaṅkas, vultures, and the like do not devour those who are alive—this too is likewise [due to the rod]. That serpents and snakes, though consisting entirely of the poison of their wrath, do not all together bite every living creature, is the efficacy of the rod.

Therefore, this praise is spoken: even the gods and others, whether possessing great supernatural power or being insentient, do not deviate from their own boundaries out of fear; how much less so human beings? Regarding this, a verse was recited by the ancients:
"But seeing the wretchedness of the forest *pāṭala* trees, and the bold blossoming of the *kuṭaja* as a mockery..."
"By giving him a connection, even a low person will surely strike at his weak point"—thus he laughed. (7.23)
All social classes would become corrupt and all moral boundaries would be shattered;
moreover, there would be universal upheaval in the world due to the misuse of punishment. (7.24)

The failure of punishment consists in its non-application or its application unjustly. When that occurs, all social classes (*varṇas*) would become corrupted, because the intermingling of castes (*saṃkara*) proceeds through illicit sexual intercourse with one another's women. The "dams" are the boundaries; all of these would be breached. The meaning is that there would be a total dissolution of all boundaries. Furthermore, Brāhmaṇas would behave like Śūdras, and Śūdras like Brāhmaṇas. Consequently, there would be universal disorder in the world; even the three worlds would no longer benefit one another through rain, heat, and so forth. (7.24)
Where the dark-hued, red-eyed Punisher, the destroyer of evil, moves about, there the subjects do not go astray, provided that the leader perceives rightly. (7.25)

These two are most praiseworthy among men; therefore, he praises the staff by means of a metaphorical description of its non-existence. The staff is of two forms: it bestows suffering and it bestows fear. Its quality as a cause of fear is due to its blackness, and its quality as a cause of suffering is due to its red eyes. The praise of the staff is thus concluded. The staff must necessarily be employed, and that [employment] depends upon the place and other factors; all else is merely explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

If there is a leader: the leader is the guide of the rod [of punishment]. If he perceives rightly, having carefully considered the place, time, and other factors, he protects [the people]. In that case, the subjects do not become deluded and are not afflicted by any fault. (7.25)
They say that its promulgator was a king who spoke the truth,
who acted with circumspection, who was wise, and who was skilled in the matters of dharma, pleasure, and wealth.

This is the excellent vision of the one who administers justice: truthfulness, acting with circumspection, wisdom, and skill in the three aims of life (*trivarga*). He is a speaker of truth when, by following the scriptures, he inflicts punishment and—upon learning that someone possesses great wealth—does not increase that penalty, nor does he show leniency toward a favorite out of favoritism. He is wise when he knows the specific circumstances regarding the relationship of subordination and predominance among place (*deśa*) and the other factors. Sometimes place is overridden by time, or time by place; sometimes both are superseded by knowledge or power. He understands the mutual relationship between these two as general rule (*utsarga*) and exception (*apavāda*). Because of the requirements of a particular task, even a factor that is normally predominant may be made subordinate; thus, wisdom is essential. Furthermore, there is the relative weight of dharma and the other aims. Where dharma is of little importance and its fulfillment would result in great harm, dharma is abandoned. One must understand such matters as how they will be rectified through expiation (*prāyaścitta*), and so forth. (7.26)
A king who administers that [punishment] properly prospers through the three aims of life;
but one who is blinded by passion, unjust, or base is destroyed by that very punishment.

By inflicting punishment with impartiality toward both enemy and friend, one prospers. One who is blinded by desire is dominated by passion; one who is uneven is prone to anger; and one who is base is intent on seeking out pretexts. Such a person is destroyed by that very punishment, either through the provocation of his subjects or by some unseen fault. (7.27)
For punishment is a very great power, difficult to be wielded by those who have not disciplined their souls;
it destroys the king himself, along with his kinsmen, if he deviates from righteousness.

That which is his great majesty is his *daṇḍa* (the rod of punishment). It is difficult to wield for those of undisciplined soul—those who have not been properly trained through the scriptures, through service to their teachers, or through innate humility; by such persons it cannot be rightly administered. One should not think: "Punishment is administered by mere command; what is so difficult about that? For the *daṇḍa* destroys the negligent man, along with his kinsmen, if he does not remain vigilant therein and does not exert effort. A king is not destroyed by his body alone, but together with his lineage of sons, grandsons, and descendants. (7.28)
Then he would afflict the fortresses, the kingdom, and the world with all its moving and unmoving beings,
as well as the sages and the gods dwelling in the intermediate space.

Wherever punishment is inflicted regardless of the location and other factors, there is the destruction of the kingdom along with its king, including its animals and stationary beings. Therefore, the king should be petitioned by the ministers and the subjects, or such a region should be abandoned. The gods and sages are being oppressed; for the gods subsist on offerings from here, and since the performance of rituals and so forth will be cut off in this [region], the gods and sages are indeed ruined. And thus it has been said by the authors of the Purāṇas:
"He who conducts himself in this world while remaining established in the system of the castes and stages of life..."
"He is indeed remembered as the cause of the stability of those born of divine origin in heaven and other realms.

From the first verse up to this verse, the summary of the meaning is as follows: A Kṣatriya who maintains impartiality must protect the inhabited lands. And since that protection cannot be achieved without punishment, he must necessarily determine it with great care in consideration of the country and other factors, and apply it according to the scriptures within his own kingdom or in foreign kingdoms. Otherwise, if he acts differently, there will be destruction in both worlds. All else is merely explanatory praise (arthavāda). (7.29)
He cannot be led by right means by one who is without a companion, who is deluded, greedy, of unformed intellect, and attached to the objects of the senses. (7.30)

This section is now commenced for the purpose of gathering assistants. For one who lacks those endowed with the qualities of assistants and so forth—namely, noble courtiers (*āryasabhya*), generals, and magistrates—the administration of justice cannot be carried out properly and without hesitation, even if he himself is fully possessed of the qualities of leadership and the [proper] time. "Justice" (*nyāya*) is a settlement in accordance with the scriptures and with regard to the specific place and other factors. Therefore, excellent assistants must be appointed. The intended meaning is that just as one who is himself deluded, distracted, of unrefined intellect, attached to sense-objects, or greedy—and thus fails to employ wealth correctly—is not able to maintain [justice] properly due to being possessed of such faults, so too is it impossible for one who is without assistants. However, one who is the opposite [of these defects] is capable [of doing so]. (7.30)
This very same point is stated by way of its opposite:
"Punishment can be administered by one who is pure, true to his word, who follows the scriptures, possesses good assistants, and is wise. (7.31)

Pure and free from greed; faithful to his word and preeminent in truth; he engages in all activities placing truth alone at the forefront—he is one who has conquered his senses. For one whose senses are unconquered, whence can there be truth? He follows and acts in accordance with the scriptures. "Having good companions" means those whose companions are excellent; he is joined by companions who are not foolish and who are devoted and loyal. "By the wise" means by the intelligent; this is stated as the opposite of that which was previously called "foolish."

Therefore, the meaning of these two verses is that one who is free from the five defects and endowed with those very same virtues is authorized to administer punishment and partakes in an abundance of both visible and invisible rewards. || 7.31 ||
He should conduct himself with justice within his own kingdom, be severe in punishment toward enemies,
straightforward toward friends, and endowed with patience toward Brahmins.

A country inherited through the succession of fathers and grandfathers is the basis for one’s designation; for a Kashmiri, it is Kashmir, and for a Pāñcāla, it is the Pāñcālas—this is one’s own kingdom. Therein, one who is of righteous conduct (*nyāyavṛtta*) should act with justice. Conduct (*vṛtta*) arises from the application of justice (*nyāya*); thus, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Alternatively, the reading may be *nyāyavṛttiḥ*. Having restated this as something already established, the imposition of severe punishment upon enemies is now enjoined. One should, moreover, afflict the kingdoms of others; in that regard, obstacles and the like are not to be overlooked, nor is the oppression of the local population. For one who acts in this manner, majesty (*pratāpa*) arises. To one whose wealth is majesty, enemies bow down. Toward Brahmins everywhere, he should be endowed with forgiveness. Even in cases of offense, punishment should be applied with conciliation, not with anger. Even inhabitants of foreign kingdoms, if they can be protected at the time of the destruction of the realm, should not be killed. Toward affectionate friends, he should be straightforward, meaning free from crookedness of mind. He should be intent on accomplishing their business and focused on their affairs. Friends are those who share in both prosperity and adversity and are affectionate. (7.32)
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even if he lives by gleaning ears of grain,
his fame spreads throughout the world like a drop of oil upon the water.

This is a praise of one who has adopted the proper course of conduct: even for one who lives by gleaning ears of grain and whose treasury is utterly depleted, his fame spreads and becomes renowned; consequently, foreign kingdoms submit of their own accord, and the subjects of his own kingdom remain steadfast out of affection. (7.33)
But for a king who acts in the opposite manner and has not conquered himself, his fame in the world diminishes like a drop of clarified butter upon water. (7.34)

Therefore, for one who has deviated from this conduct, there is instability; the cause of this is the lack of self-mastery. One whose self is not disciplined according to the scriptures [is such a person]. (7.34)
The king was created as the protector of all the social classes and stages of life, who are each established in their respective duties in due order. (7.35)

The king was created as the protector of those who abide by their own duties (*svadharma*). There is sin for the king if he fails to protect those established in their own duties. However, if those who have fallen from *dharma* are harmed by someone, the king is not excessively at fault; this is what is shown by the phrase "in their respective duties. Alternatively, the word "not" (*na*) connects with "those who are not settled" (*aniviṣṭānām*). As for those who are dependent on their own duties due to the scriptures or the instruction of friends and others, the king should not treat them with duplicity. The mention of "castes" (*varṇa*) is for the purpose of protecting women, children, and the elderly, for they are not residents of the stages of life (*āśrama*). If so, for what purpose is the mention of "stages of life"? It is for the sake of emphasizing importance, like the case of Brāhmaṇas and Vasiṣṭha. Or, this is an indication of the specific purpose: one must not cause these people to deviate from their duties such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) belonging to the stages of life. Nor should one allow them to suffer harm from punishment and the like. Otherwise, there would be no avoidance of distress. Thus is protection to be understood. When they fail to perform the twilight worship and other rites, no other [punishment] whatsoever may be imposed. The mention of both "castes" and "stages of life" indicates that the king’s duty is of two forms. This very point has been stated: "He shall protect the castes and the stages of life according to justice" (GDh 11.9). 7.35.
Therefore, whatever must be done by one who protects his subjects along with his retinue,
all that I shall declare to you exactly and in due order.

This verse is intended to introduce what is about to be explained. Now, that which must be done by the king together with his servants and his own assistants for the sake of protecting the subjects is being stated. (7.36)
Having risen in the morning, the king should attend upon the brahmins;
he should remain in the presence of those who are learned and advanced in the knowledge of the three Vedas, and abide by their instruction. (7.37)

Having risen in the morning, left his bed, and performed the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*) according to the rules, he should first seek the sight of Brāhmaṇas. "Attendance" (*upāsana*) consists of sitting near them and engaging in inquiries regarding their welfare and so forth. *Pari* is used here as a particle to fill out the meter. He should abide by their instruction; "instruction" (*śāsana*) means carrying out their commands. If they should command him for the sake of some benefit, it should not be doubted, nor should he perform anything that would be harmful. "Those aged in the three sciences" (*traividyavṛddhān*): the collection of the three sciences is "the triple science" (*traividyam*); those who have studied that are "versed in the triple science" (*traividyāḥ*). By conventional usage, this refers to those who study the three Vedas, such as the Ṛgveda and the others. They are both learned (*viduṣaḥ*)—meaning those who know the meaning of those [Vedas]—and such Brāhmaṇas he should attend upon and carry out their commands. "Aged" (*vṛddhāḥ*) means the best among those versed in the triple science, being preeminent in both study and understanding. (7.37)
One should always serve elderly Brahmins who are pure and learned in the Vedas;
for one who constantly serves the elderly is honored even by the Rākṣasas. (7.38)

"Vṛddhān" means elderly Brahmins. This is a novel point; the other [qualification], "viprān" (Brahmins) and so forth, is already established by what precedes. "Śucīn" means those free from defects. This too is a novel point: just as proficiency in study and understanding is a cause for being worthy of worship, so too is purity. The second half of the verse is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). "By the *rakṣas*s": *rakṣas*s are merciless, possess great strength, and are devoid of all dharma; yet even they honor one who serves the elderly. (7.38)
He states the purpose of serving the elderly:
"From them he should constantly acquire discipline, even though his own self is already disciplined;
for a king whose self is disciplined never perishes" (7.39).

From those learned and aged Brahmins, he should acquire and learn discipline (*vinaya*) and the conduct of kings. Being disciplined in soul—even if he is already disciplined by his own intelligence or through the treatises on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*)—he should nevertheless exert effort in the instruction of the aged. Those who have witnessed actual practice are more skillful than those who merely know the scriptures. Alternatively, for the sake of generating an excellence of proficiency, even one who is naturally disciplined must have himself trained by aged and noble men. Just as gold that is pure by nature, when its refinement is applied through contact with fire and other means, is seen to possess an even purer form; so too is this [discipline], the fruit of which does not perish. (7.39)
Many kings, together with their retinues, have perished through lack of discipline;
yet even those dwelling in the forest have obtained kingdoms through discipline. (7.40)

The very point previously stated is further reinforced by these three verses. Those who are undisciplined and possessed of worldly attachments are ruined; "attachment" (*parigraha*) here refers to the possession of sons, wives, elephants, horses, and other such wealth. However, those who are disciplined do not lose their kingdom upon attaining it. Even when they are far away, dwelling in the forest, or even destitute of a treasury, they have attained—that is, they have gained—the kingdom. (7.40)
Vena was ruined through lack of discipline, as were King Nahuṣa, Sudās Paijavana, Sumukha, and Nimi. (7.41)
In both cases, they describe examples well-known in the world; these are to be understood as narratives from the Mahābhārata. 7.41.
Pṛthu indeed obtained the kingdom through discipline, as did Manu;
Kubera obtained mastery over wealth, and the son of Gādhi obtained the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
And Gādhija [attained] the status of a Brāhmaṇa.

Now, one might ask: what occasion is there for mentioning the attainment of Brāhmaṇahood when the context concerns the qualification for kingship? One should have described only the acquisition of the kingdom as before.
It is said in reply: even more difficult to attain than wealth and sovereignty is the excellence of birth (*jātyutkarṣa*), because it is the cause of all forms of authority.

But how is discipline (*vinaya*) the cause of that? Discipline consists of the application of the six measures of statecraft (*ṣāḍguṇya*), vigilance, avoidance of excessive expenditure, freedom from greed, refraining from vices, and so forth. Yet none of these is a cause for Brahminhood; for austerity (*tapas*) alone is heard of as the cause therein: "Viśvāmitra performed austerity, [thinking], 'May I not be the son of a non-seer,'" and so on.

It is said: Policy (*nīti*) is not merely that which is taught in treatises on worldly affairs (*arthaśāstra*). What then? It is both scriptural injunction and worldly custom. And in the scriptures, it is indeed ordained that the excellence of caste (*jātyutkarṣa*) is attained through austerity (*tapas*) in another birth. As for Viśvāmitra’s attainment of Brahminhood, it is well known that this occurred while he was still a Kṣatriya in that very same life. (7.42)

From those learned in the three Vedas, he should learn the triple Veda, the eternal science of government (daṇḍanīti), the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī), the knowledge of the self (ātmavidyā), and the various undertakings of trade from the people. (7.43)

In the reading where *vidyām* ends in the accusative case, the word *adhigacchet* (from MDh 7.39) should be supplied as the verb. Since the instruction regarding kingship is given for one who has completed his period of Vedic studentship (*brahmacarya*), and since that [kingship] is accomplished through the mastery of the meaning of the three Vedas, this instruction is intended for the purpose of practice. "Threefold knowledge" (*trividyā*) refers to that which consists of three parts; those who study it are called *traividyāḥ*. From them, he should learn the *trayī*, the triad of Vedas beginning with the Ṛgveda. He should effect a determination regarding doubtful matters from the Vedas; that is to say, he should contemplate the meaning of the Vedas together with them. He should not, out of pride in his royal status or through the arrogance of intoxication, neglect doubtful matters with the thought, "I am omniscient."

And the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*). Government is the policy regarding punishment. As it is said: "They say that *daṇḍa* is subduing" (GDh 11.28). That by which enemies, one's own subjects, and the inhabitants of the realm who act unjustly are subdued is *daṇḍa*; this consists of the excellence of ministers and other officials. *Nīti* is its application—the rule therein—and he should learn that from those who know it, such as those learned in the treatises of Cāṇakya and others. The word "eternal" (*śāśvatīm*) is a praise. Although even through the science of government the entire world can be understood—since this subject matter is rooted in positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—nevertheless, those scriptures are intended for the instruction of the ignorant and for the mutual corroboration of the wise; thus, the mastery of the science of government is appropriate.

In this way, *ānvīkṣikī* is also the science of logic (*tarka-vidyā*), the treatises on statecraft (*artha-śāstra*), and so forth. *Ātmavidyā* is the science of the inner self (*adhyātma-vidyā*). Alternatively, these are two distinct terms: the former being the object of knowledge and the latter the subject. That *ānvīkṣikī* which is beneficial for the self is based upon logic; one should study it. For it is useful for the cessation of vice and prosperity-seeking, and for the pacification of mental agitation. However, that science of logic belonging to the Buddhists, Cārvākas, and others is of little use anywhere; on the contrary, it destroys one's faith, especially for those whose intellects are not very refined. But when one knows *ānvīkṣikī* as an independent discipline, then its utility in matters such as diplomatic correspondence and the clarity of speech does not become an object of ridicule.

And [he should learn] the undertakings of the means of livelihood (*vārtā*). The thorough knowledge of the value of commodities and skill in trade—understanding these according to the *Bārhaspatya* manual—is "livelihood" (*vārtā*). Undertakings based on that are "undertakings of livelihood" (*vārtārambhāḥ*). Having understood the nature of livelihood, the engagement in activities concerning it is an "undertaking. One should learn this from the world; by "the world" here, those who live by trade are intended, for they are skilled in that matter. And the phrase "from the world" should be applied as a supplement to the two preceding [items]. Consequently, it follows that in all cases [one learns] "from those who know it. (7.43)
One should apply oneself day and night to the conquest of the senses;
for one who has conquered the senses is able to keep the subjects under control. (7.44)

The victory over the senses (*indriyajaya*), which has been taught as the foremost goal for all human beings among the duties of a religious student (*brahmacārin*), is taught here once again in order to indicate that this discipline (*vinaya*) is the primary duty of a king. This is what he says with the words "one who has conquered his senses," and so forth. This is well known to everyone: the subjects do not remain under the control of one whose senses are unconquered. *Yoga* means application; [this applies] day and night, throughout the twenty-four hours. (7.44)
One should diligently avoid the ten vices arising from desire and the eight born of anger, which have miserable ends. (7.45)

This is another purpose for the instruction on the conquest of the senses: for one whose senses are unconquered, calamities are difficult to avoid. They have a miserable end—that is, their conclusion or termination is full of suffering. Calamities bring pleasure at the time they first arise, but afterwards they produce bitterness; therefore, they are called "miserable ends. Alternatively, their end is difficult to reach, for those beset by calamities are unable to turn back from them. Their origin or birth is from the cause of desire. (7.45)

He states the purpose for avoiding these, as well as their relative gravity: "For a lord of the earth who is addicted to vices born of desire is deprived of both wealth and dharma; but one addicted to those born of anger is deprived of his very self. (7.46)
Through the loss of wealth and virtue, one is separated from oneself; however, the distinction regarding those [sins] born of anger is that one is separated from everything. (7.46)
He now shows those vices by their own names:
hunting, gambling, sleeping during the day, slander, women, intoxication, the triple symphony [of song, dance, and instrument], and idle wandering—this is the tenfold group born of desire. (7.47)

Hunting (*ākheṭaka*) is the killing of wild animals; gambling (*akṣa*) is play centered upon them. The harmful nature of these two is well known. Day-sleep (*divāsvapna*) is the failure to engage in duties during the time for performing them. By the word "day," the daytime itself is not necessarily intended; as it is said: "Those who are fast asleep when they ought to be awake" (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.49.31). Alternatively, day-sleep refers to sleeping during the actual daytime; for that is forbidden and obstructs all activities. Furthermore, among subjects, it generates resentment because others who wish to see [the king] do not obtain that opportunity. Slander (*parivāda*) is the divulging of another's faults in secret. Through this, all the constituent elements of the state (*prakṛtis*) become alienated; and in slandering those who should not be slandered, unrighteousness (*adharma*) is certainly established. The harmful nature of women and intoxication is well understood. The triple symphony (*tauryatrika*) consists of dancing, singing, and instrumental music. Idle wandering (*vṛthāṭyā*) is roaming here and there without purpose or with only slight purpose. "Tenfold" (*daśaka*) means having ten as its measure. "Born of desire" (*kāmaja*): desire (*kāma*) is longing; that from which something is born is "born of desire. Alternatively, it is "born of desire" because it arises for the sake of enjoying specific pleasures or from the memory of previously experienced excellence. (7.47)
Slander, violence, malice, envy, finding fault, and the corruption of wealth, as well as harshness of speech and severity of punishment—this is the eightfold group born of anger. (7.48)

Regarding ministers and others [46], those who are well-disposed toward their kin, whatever ought to be concealed therein, its disclosure constitutes slander (*paiśunya*). Violence (*sāhasa*) consists in the employment of a superior in a base task, or the imposition of taxes or imprisonment for even a slight offense. Malice (*droha*) is secret killing or injury while the victim is still alive. Envy (*īrṣyā*) is the exclusion of another from a common object of enjoyment, or an inability to endure it. Spite (*asūyā*) is the revelation of faults in the virtues of those possessed of merit. Embezzlement (*arthadūṣaṇa*) is the non-payment or the seizure of wealth. Harshness of speech and severity of punishment are well known. Anger (*krodha*) is hatred; those dominated by these [vices] perform such acts. (7.48)
One should strive to conquer that greed which all poets know to be the root of both these; for from it both these classes arise.

It has already been stated that greed (*lobha*) is the root of the category of vices born of desire (*kāmajavyasana*). Since desire (*kāma*) is the longing for the enjoyment of sense objects, and greed (*lobha*) is synonymous with wish (*icchā*) and aspiration (*abhilāṣa*), there is no difference in meaning between them. However, how is greed the root of those born of anger (*krodhaja*), such that it is said, "both these two groups arise from that"?

It is said: it is not intended here that greed is the cause of those two groups [of vices]. What then? Greed is equal to both groups. For greed alone produces that very same harm which all these vices produce, even for one who is otherwise free from vice. Thus it is said: "Greed [destroys] all virtues" (MBh 7.74.537). Therefore, this was stated figuratively: "these two arise from that. If greed were not produced, how could they have identical results? For a defect in the cause manifests as a defect in the effect. Thus, if there is a defect in the vices because they are its effects, then certainly that defect is also attributed to the cause.

Alternatively, it is the greedy person alone who develops an attachment to such things as slander—which are to be shunned—while the other [the passionate person] is appeased by conciliation even regarding a very slight object. Thus, this two-fold category of vices is said to have its root in greed through figurative usage.
Drinking, dice, women, and hunting—one should know this quartet to be the most grievous in the group of vices born of desire, in their respective order. (7.50)
It is well known that this group of four, beginning with sleeping during the day, possesses a far greater degree of fault. 7.50.
One should know that this triad—inflicting physical punishment, verbal abuse, and the embezzlement of wealth—is always difficult to endure, even within the group of vices born of anger. (7.51)
It is well known that this triad is even more evil than slander and the like. 7.51.
A self-possessed person should know that among this group of seven vices which are everywhere interconnected, each preceding one is more grievous than the next. (7.52)

Between drinking and gambling, drinking is the more serious vice. For in it there is the loss of consciousness; the becoming insane for one who is not insane; the becoming a ghost for one who is not a ghost; the exposure of one's private parts; the abandonment of learning and wisdom; the loss of friends; separation from the virtuous and association with the wicked; addiction to singing and other pursuits that destroy wealth; the disclosure of secrets and counsel; being made an object of ridicule even by those who respect him; and, due to the force of intoxication, the speaking of whatever comes to mind even by one of a profound nature—these are the faults of drinking. In gambling, however, victory belongs to the one skilled in dice, while for one ignorant of the game, defeat is merely a matter of chance.

Between the two vices of women and gambling, the vice of gambling is more serious. For even the very wealth won by it becomes poison to him; likewise, victory resulting from it leads to a persistent chain of enmity, while defeat is common to all and results merely in the loss of what has been enjoyed. Furthermore, the suppression of the urges of urine and feces causes physical debility, which is indeed the primary cause of disease; because of this, one suffers extreme affliction even from minor ailments. Even when his mother has died, he continues to gamble. When his purposes are accomplished, he cannot be dissuaded even by friends. He does not trust those who handle the wealth of others as if it were a red-hot iron ball. Even if he is endowed with every virtue, he becomes an object of neglect like a blade of grass to the hungry and the destitute who seek food and drink. Such are the faults of gambling. In the case of the vice of women, however, there is the procreation of offspring, the enjoyment of personal adornment and abundant food, and the acquisition of merit and wealth. Moreover, a woman can be employed for the king’s welfare or even used to lure away an enemy.

Between the two vices of women and hunting, the vice of women is more serious. [It leads to] the neglect of duties, indifference toward royal affairs due to attachment to the vice of women, the wasting of time, the loss of dharma, the persistence of the evils of drinking, and addiction to falsehood and other vices that destroy wealth. In hunting, however, there is physical exercise, the binding of bile and phlegm, the reduction of fat and other humors, familiarity with targets whether moving or stationary, the development of skill in weaponry, and the subduing of rustic people.
Thus, within this group of four born of desire, each preceding one is more evil than the next.
Furthermore, for that which is born of anger, there is the consequence of the fault of striking with a rod, as well as attachment to falsehood and other such acts that destroy wealth.

Between striking with a rod and verbal abuse, striking with a rod is the graver offense. For in the case of striking with a rod, the destruction of the body and so forth can be remedied; however, in the case of verbal abuse, the fire of anger born of impatience can be extinguished by the waters of gifts and honors.

Between verbal abuse and the destruction of property, verbal abuse is more serious. For those possessed of spirit do not experience fear when their minds are agitated by harsh words. Thus runs the proverb: "An arrow, firm and well-whetted, having pierced through bone and entered the marrow, may leave the body free of its shaft; but words do not depart even from the heart."
A forest pierced by arrows or struck down by an axe grows back again;
but the wound caused by speech, O Bībhatsu, never heals when harsh words have been spoken.

"Since wealth depends upon fortune, those possessed of splendor do not count the spoiling of wealth as a fault. Thus, the greater importance of each preceding category over the subsequent one has been demonstrated for these two groups.
Between vice and death, vice is said to be the more grievous;
the man of vice sinks lower and lower, while the man free from vice goes to heaven when he dies.

Even though both death and vice may take everything away, there is nevertheless this distinction: death takes all in this world alone, whereas vice takes everything in both this world and the next. Thus it is said: "The man of vice sinks lower and lower," which means he goes to hell. By the word *vyasani* (the addicted person), an excessive habit regarding these [vices] is expressed; therefore, what is prohibited here is such habitual indulgence, not a slight degree of practice. For these things, when they become vices, destroy the virtue, wealth, pleasure, and life of even an ordinary person, let alone a king. Furthermore, total abstinence from drinking and the like is improper and impossible; hence, what is forbidden is their habitual practice. (7.53)
He should appoint seven or eight ministers who are hereditary, learned in the treatises, brave, skilled in hitting the mark, of noble birth, and thoroughly tested. (7.54)

Those who have descended through a lineage of fathers and grandfathers; who possess many sons, wealth, and kinsmen; whose cattle, lands, and riches are manifest; who are indigenous inhabitants of that region (*maula*); *mūla* means foundation or established status, and those existing therein are the *maula*. They are experts in the *śāstra*. *Śāstra* here refers to governance and the knowledge of managing servants; by this term, other qualities are also included, as follows: "He should be wise, firm in action, retentive, dexterous, eloquent, powerful, resourceful, endowed with energy and majesty, capable of enduring hardship, pure, generous, possessed of a fit character, free from arrogance and fickleness, beloved [by his people], and one who does not act against his enemies" (cf. *Arthaśāstra* 1.9.1). By the word "hero" (*śūra*), one who is indifferent even toward body, wife, children, and wealth for the sake of the king's business is meant. Likewise, one who is fearless in death, enthusiastic for battle, who alone opposes many out of fear of humiliation, who strikes firmly, and is strong. He should be one who has attained his mark. By this, he declares that his work has been observed. He should be one who has seen the application of the sword, who has fulfilled his duties, and who has experienced the stages of ministerial office. Those born of noble families, restrained by the "goad" of their lineage, do not engage in improper acts. These should be ministers, companions, who should always remain by the king’s side—either seven or eight; this is the rule, so that they may be few in number and of one mind. Otherwise, the king's counsel would be leaked, and there would be a breach of secrecy among many. Therefore, only this many should be appointed. They must be well-tested through the trials of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and fear. This testing is described as follows: The *Purohita* (family priest)—having been falsely accused by the king on some minor pretext—should, through trusted men and the offering of much wealth, instigate each individual minister to destroy the king, saying: "This is pleasing to all the ministers; what do you think? If he rejects it, he is proven pure by the trial of virtue (*dharmopadhā*). The *Senāpati* (commander-in-chief)—having been falsely accused under some pretext as before, and offered much wealth by trusted men—should instigate each individual minister to destroy the king, saying: "This is pleasing to all the ministers; what do you think? If he rejects it, he is proven pure by the trial of wealth (*arthopadhā*). A female ascetic (*parivrājikā*) who has gained confidence in the harem should instigate each individual minister, saying: "That queen desires you and has already arranged a meeting. If he rejects it, he is proven pure by the trial of pleasure (*kāmopadhā*). Certain men employed by the king should spread a rumor: "The king is being killed by the ministers who have made a pact. Upon learning this rumor, a trusted agent of the *Purohita* should whisper the counsel among the ministers, saying: "Having heard this rumor, the king intends to punish you. Then, one of those very men, having previously made an agreement, should incite each of the royal ministers individually. Among them, those who refuse are proven pure by the trial of fear (*bhayopadhā*).

Alternatively, he should first appoint hereditary officials (*maula*) as collectors of revenue (*arthasamāhartṛ*) and treasurers (*saṃnidhātṛ*). These are those who collect wealth from the villages, protect what has been collected, and disburse it. The meaning is that, in every respect, those who manage financial affairs must be hereditary officials; this is what is being stated. "Experts in the treatises" refers to the ministers who are counselors for intelligence (*buddhisaciva*). "Brave men" refers to the commanders of the army. "Those who have hit the mark" and so forth are adjectives qualifying all of them. Regarding the statement that the examination of each individual should be conducted collectively concerning the king's domain—that is, the instigation of the king’s ministers—some consider that to be improper. For that would indeed cause a division of counsel among the ministers. Therefore, some other virtuous woman should be employed, and another example involving ruin should be cited. (7.54)
Even an action that is easy to perform is difficult for one person alone to accomplish, especially without assistance; how much more so is a kingdom of great consequence? (7.55)

It is established that the common household duties of a householder—such as the easy task of tending cattle, horses, and so forth—are manageable; yet it is he alone who tends the cow and he alone who milks it. This cannot be accomplished by one person alone, and it is especially difficult for one without assistance. What is difficult cannot be performed by one who lacks the capacity. For how can one person alone pasture the cattle, and how can he protect his wife? Moreover, sovereignty involves great undertakings and the labor of generating revenue; its application is fruitful, and for one who looks toward it, great results arise. Furthermore, the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) cannot be understood by one person alone. Therefore, assistants who have been tested and found equal to oneself should be employed in various tasks. (7.55)
Together with them, he should constantly deliberate upon common matters: peace and war, stability, revenue, protection, and the consolidation of what has been acquired. (7.56)

Together with those chief ministers of intelligence and officials in charge of affairs, he should deliberate upon peace and war—specifically that which is not highly secret—considering: "Is peace appropriate at this time, or is it war? He should examine the merits and defects in both cases. However, he should determine what must be done by his own intellect, so that he does not become subject to the influence of others.

Furthermore, he should consider this other matter: the *sthāna* (the state or domain). That is fourfold: the army (*daṇḍa*), the treasury (*kośa*), the city (*pura*), and the kingdom (*rāṣṭra*). Among these, the army consists of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. One must consider their maintenance, nourishment, protection, and so forth; for indeed, a lack of preparedness is not primary. Likewise, regarding the treasury, one must consider the abundance of gold and silver, the prevalence of silver, and the characteristics of income and expenditure. Whatever sources of income there are for the treasury, they must not be squandered nor delayed for the sake of the servants. Similarly, regarding the kingdom—which is synonymous with the country—one must consider whether it provides a livelihood for oneself and sustenance for others; whether it contains rivers and trees, is suitable for cattle, is largely free from enemies and hateful intruders, has secure pastures, is rich in livestock, does not depend solely on rain, and is capable of supporting the army and taxes in times of distress, and so forth. Regarding the city, the author will say later: "It should be well-equipped with weapons" (MDh 7.75).

Alternatively, "position" (*sthāna*) refers to not being displaced from one's own territory. In this manner, the entire collection [of topics] should also be considered. Among these, agriculture, cattle-pens, and plantations, as well as trade, customs duties, and fines, and so forth; the protection of one's own kingdom will be explained later. The pacification of what has been acquired consists of the honoring, giving of gifts, and bestowing of exemptions upon deities, hermitages, the learned, and the righteous, as well as the granting of permissions to those who are accustomed [to such privileges]. It includes the release of all prisoners and the favoring of the distressed and the diseased. Furthermore, it involves the inauguration of unprecedented festivals and the continuation of those already established.

Having removed any unrighteous conduct that undermines the treasury and the army, he should establish legal proceedings according to the Dharma. He should not allow unrighteous conduct—whether previously uncommitted or committed by others—to proceed, nor should he allow what has been done righteously by others to be overturned.
In this manner, the locations and other factors are to be considered. 7.56.
Having ascertained each of their individual intentions,
he should act for his own benefit regarding the affairs of all of them together.

Having ascertained the individual secret intentions and the thoughts held in the hearts of each one of them separately, he should ask all of them together about the reason why a certain man might be lacking in presence of mind in an assembly yet bold in private, or why another might have attained wisdom in an assembly. Then, he himself should determine and carry out that which is more appropriate and beneficial for himself. Its authority rests in what has been taught by any one of those very individuals, provided it is not contradictory and is free from fault. (7.57)
But the king should deliberate upon the supreme counsel, endowed with the sixfold policy, together with all his ministers and especially with a learned Brāhmaṇa.

A wise man, learned and conversant with the treatises on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*), should deliberate upon a supreme counsel—one that is strictly to be kept secret and endowed with the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*). For a Brahmin possesses superior wisdom, and because of his righteousness, he is trustworthy. (7.58)
Always placing one's trust in him, one should entrust all affairs to him;
having deliberated with him, one should then undertake the task. (7.59)

Having entrusted the entire circle of the kingdom to such a brahmin, the king may enjoy the pleasures of sovereignty with full confidence. Having reached a firm decision together with him, he should carry out activities such as traveling and sitting, as well as the administration of legal affairs and the collection of revenues. (7.59)
He should also appoint other ministers who are pure, wise, steadfast, well-tested, and capable of properly collecting revenue. (7.60)

This is an exception to what was stated [in MDh 7.54]: "Seven or eight. He should appoint collectors of revenue and treasurers who have been thoroughly tested by means of secret trials (*upadhā*). 7.60.
He should appoint as many men—vigilant, skillful, and discerning—as may be required to carry out his duties. (7.61)

All these should be appointed as experts in mantras, discerning, learned, and authorized; they should be capable, possessing great perseverance even when faced with fear or causes for despondency; and they should be untiring and free from laziness. And it is said in the *Adhyakṣapracāra*:
"He whose minister is intelligent, loyal, diligent, skilled in matters of dharma and artha, pure, capable, and of noble birth, shall possess the kingdom."
Having entrusted his affairs to him, one who is attached to enjoyments does not perish; for by means of gifts and favors, he [the minister] carries out the king's commands. (7.61)
For their sake, he should employ those who are brave, capable, and of noble birth at the mines and in the workshops;
and those who are pure and timid within the inner apartments.

Regarding "in matters" (arthe), it means in the administration of income and expenditure. One should appoint those who are pure and free from greed to these matters. He illustrates these financial positions with examples, namely "mines and manufactories" (ākarakarmānta). Mines are places for the extraction and refinement of gold, silver, and so forth; manufactories include the production of foodstuffs, cotton, seeds, and the like. "In the inner apartments" (antarveśmane) refers to the harem, the dining hall, the bedchamber, and the women's quarters. Cowards should be appointed there, for brave men, if instigated by enemies, might kill the king when he is alone. Furthermore, all those who are capable—by virtue of their energetic nature and disregard for personal risk in conflict—do not allow their master’s business to be delayed beyond its proper time. (7.62)
And he should appoint as a messenger one who is learned in all the scriptures,
who understands gestures, facial expressions, and movements, and who is pure, capable, and of noble birth.

This is the preeminent quality of an envoy: the knowledge of gestures, facial expressions, and physical movements. When a king or his ministers desire to form an alliance with another state, they attentively observe the envoy’s gestures, grant him full reception, place their trust in him, and repeatedly welcome his complete statements. One should disregard these qualities if they appear in reverse. *Ākāra* (facial expression) refers to bodily distortions, such as a pale face, a change in complexion, silence, or long, hot sighs. Through such transformations, one indicates dejection: “He has met with some misfortune; that is why he is so discolored. Confidence in speech, physical grooming, and a cheerful countenance indicate joy. Regarding purity (*śuci*), it concerns matters involving women through specific modes of conduct, because in dealings with women there is the risk of leaking secret counsel and suffering humiliation. (7.63)
Loyal, pure, skillful, mindful, and knowing place and time; handsome, fearless, and eloquent—a messenger such as this is praised by kings. (7.64)

Being devoted, he is incorruptible. Being skillful, he does not transgress [the rules of] place and time. Being mindful, through his unimpaired memory, he recounts the master’s message exactly as it was entrusted to him. Knowing the proper place and time, having understood them, he speaks even that which was not specifically instructed, provided it is appropriate for that occasion. Being handsome and well-formed, he speaks skillfully and appropriately because of his pleasing appearance. Being free from fear, he speaks with confidence. Being eloquent, he is capable of providing a reply to the response to the message. (7.64)

He states the purpose for the effort to accomplish the qualities of an envoy already mentioned: "The army depends upon the minister; the administration of justice depends upon the army; the treasury and the kingdom depend upon the king; and peace and its opposite depend upon the envoy. (7.65)

The *daṇḍa* (the power of punishment) depends upon the minister and the commander-in-chief, because it is through their will that one proceeds with affairs; therein lies the *vainayikī* (the policy of discipline). For whoever is to be disciplined—whether residing in one's own kingdom or in a foreign realm—is to be punished, since discipline is based upon such subjugation. "Action" refers to the task to be performed. The treasury (*kośa*) and the realm (*rāṣṭra*) depend upon the king. The treasury is the place of accumulation; the realm is the inhabited territory. These two must not be made dependent on others, as they yield fruit when managed by oneself alone. Alliance (*saṃdhi*) and its opposite (*vigraha*, war) depend upon the envoy. Through pleasant speech and the demonstration of the master’s interests, there is alliance; through the reverse of that, there is conflict. Both of these are dependent upon the envoy. (7.65)
Such is the messenger’s repetition of the purpose. This very point is stated again:
"For it is the messenger alone who unites and indeed divides those who are united;
the messenger performs that action by which men are divided. (7.66)

The messenger [98] brings about an alliance as previously described; he himself breaks apart those who have allied and become one. He conveys pleasant messages even when they were not requested, such as "he has acted contrary to you," and so forth. He speaks of gold and other wealth that was never promised. In this way the messenger creates division. This is the method taught for the "intermediate act" (*karmāntara*) by which kings are divided. [99] It is through the occurrence of harsh speech that such things come to pass. (7.66)
He also shows another duty of a messenger:
"By means of secret hints, gestures, and movements, he should discern his [the king's] facial expression, hint, and gesture, as well as what he intends to do regarding his servants. (7.67)
Having understood in its true essence everything intended by the enemy king, one should apply such effort as will not cause oneself suffering. (7.68)
That messenger [was engaged] in the duties and affairs of King Yātavya.

One should dwell in a country that is arid yet rich in crops, predominantly inhabited by noble people, free from turmoil, delightful, with submissive vassals, and where a livelihood is easily obtained. (7.69)
Having taken refuge in a desert fort, an earth fort, a water fort, a forest fort, a human fort, or a mountain fort, he should dwell in his city. (7.70)

A *mahīdurga* (earth-fort) is one surrounded by a rampart made of bricks or stone, twice as high as it is wide, rising more than twelve cubits from the ground, with a base like a palm tree and a summit crowned by battlements (*kapiśīrṣa*), and provided with a strong drainage system. An *abdurga* (water-fort) is one encircled by a deep and unfordable moat. A *vārkṣadurga* (tree-fort) is one extending for half a *yojana* in every direction, filled with dense, massive trees. A *nṛdurga* (human-fort) is one occupied by a fourfold army and consisting mostly of heroic men equipped with excellent weapons. A *giridurga* (hill-fort) is one situated on a mountain ridge that is difficult to ascend, accessible by only a single path, and containing water from internal rivers and springs. (7.70)
But with every effort, one should take refuge in a mountain fort;
for by virtue of its many advantages, the mountain fort is distinguished above all others.
Of these, the first three are inhabited respectively by wild beasts, by those dwelling in pits, and by Apsarases; the latter three are inhabited respectively by monkeys, humans, and gods. (7.72)

The first three are the fortresses consisting of mountains and so forth. "Those who have taken refuge" means those who have made them their dwelling place: wild animals; those who dwell in holes, such as gargaras and mongooses; and those who dwell in water, such as crocodiles and tortoises. This is for the purpose of demonstrating that whatever qualities and defects these fortresses and their inhabitants possess, the same apply to kings as well. The latter three are the following: monkeys (plavaṅgamas). || 7.72 ||
Just as enemies do not harm those who have taken refuge in a fortress, so too do foes not harm a king who has taken refuge in a fortress. (7.73)

This verse concerns the purpose of constructing fortifications. Even those with very small forces, when relying on a fortress, cannot be easily overcome by enemies of great strength; therefore, taking refuge in a fortress is appropriate. (7.73)
A single archer standing upon a rampart can fight a hundred; a hundred can fight ten thousand. Therefore, a fortress is ordained. (7.74)
This purpose of a fort is well known:
by the example of a rampart, it is understood that this refers to the strength of a mountain fort (*giridurga*).
That is incorrect, because a rampart is also possible in the case of an earth fort (*mahīdurga*). Therefore, the purpose of all forts is to be determined by one's own intelligence. (7.74)
That [city] shall be well-provided with weapons, wealth, grain, and vehicles; with Brahmins, artisans, and machines; and with fodder and water. (7.75)

"Equipped with weapons" means provided with swords, spears, and the like. The mention of "weapons" is intended to indicate other implements of war as well, such as armor, helmets, and equipment. "Wealth" refers to silver, gold, and so forth. "Vehicles" refers to chariots, horses, and the like. "By artisans" means by those who operate machines, carpenters, and others. "With fodder. "By Brāhmaṇas" means by ministers, domestic priests, or others. By the phrase "with a banner and a small flag," it is sometimes implied that they proceed with the assistance of royal authority; furthermore, because this is illustrative, one should also expect physicians, medicines, and so on, and whatever is useful for healing and the like should be kept ready. (7.75)
In the center of that [site], he should have his own house constructed—spacious, well-protected against all seasons, bright, and provided with water and trees. (7.76)

It should be well-provided with everything necessary, as much as required for the king’s own use, including the royal treasury, armory, stables for horses, and so forth. He should have a house built that is secure and consists of many chambers. It should be suitable for all seasons and adorned with flowers and fruits of every season—meaning that all seasons are present there. By the word *ṛtu* (season), its effects, such as flowers and fruits, are indicated. In the reading *sarvartuga*, the etymology is "that which goes to or reaches all seasons," though the meaning remains the same: whatever exists in a place is said to be pervaded by it. It should be bright, whitened with lime, and provided with water and trees, complete with shower-houses, gardens, and groves. (7.76)
Having occupied that [seat], he should marry a wife of his own caste who possesses auspicious marks, born of a noble family, charming, and endowed with beauty and virtue. (7.77)

Having taken possession of that house, a wife should be wedded from a great family for the sake of assistance therein; this is for the purpose of protection through such a connection. That [wife] of the same caste and so forth has been previously explained. She should be "hṛdyā," meaning pleasing to the mind, endowed with radiance and charm. "Rūpa" refers to physical form; "guṇas" refer to qualities such as speech and conduct. She should be "anvitā," meaning possessed of these. (7.77)
He should appoint a domestic priest and choose officiating priests; they shall perform for him the domestic rites as well as those pertaining to the sacrificial fires. (7.78)

Even though there is no explicit mention of a second person, the singular number is intended to be significant because it is specifically stated, as in other instances such as "he cuts the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ chinatti*) and "he should marry a wife" (*bhāryāṃ vindeta*). One should choose the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); their number is to be understood from the scriptural injunction itself. And their qualifications are as follows: "Neither too stout nor too lean, neither too tall nor too short, neither too old nor too young; those whose lineage extends back seven generations on both sides through learning, austerity, and meritorious deeds; regarding them, one does not suspect non-Brahminhood, for 'the learned man performs the sacrifice,'" and so forth. Domestic rites (*gṛhyāṇi karmāṇi*) are those such as propitiatory and auspicious ceremonies. Vedic rites (*vaitānikāni*) are those pertaining to the domestic fire-altars (*tretāgni*), performed in the sacrificial hall. (7.78)
The king should sacrifice with various rituals accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees; and for the sake of dharma, he should bestow enjoyments and wealth upon the brahmins. (7.79)

By means of the Pauṇḍarīka and other sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees and large gifts, [he bestows] enjoyments and wealth.
