"Enjoyments" (bhoga) refers to garments, perfumes, ointments, and so forth, as well as varieties of food; "wealth" (dhana) refers to gold and the like. They maintain that such giving should be performed constantly, solely for the sake of Dharma and for the very purpose of its arising. (7.79)
He should cause the annual tribute to be collected from the kingdom by trusted officials,
and he should be devoted to righteous conduct in the world, behaving toward his subjects like a father.

He should collect taxes—such as a sixth or eighth part of grain and other produce—from those who have been purified by tests regarding wealth and other matters. As it has been said, he should be devoted to the traditional scriptures (*āmnāya*) and rely upon the treatises on logic that prioritize authoritative tradition (*āgama*). Alternatively, he should take only the portion that has come down through tradition and nothing more. He should behave toward his subjects like a father; he should act with a sense of affection toward both those who pay taxes and others. (7.80)
He should appoint various learned supervisors in their respective places;
they shall oversee all the affairs of the men as they carry them out. (7.81)

He should appoint supervisors (*adhyakṣāḥ*), that is, authorized overseers. These should be of various kinds—of many types, mild, fierce, righteous, and intent on the acquisition of wealth. In their respective places, such as the gold treasury, the storehouse for merchandise, and the workshops, he should station wise men who are authorized and responsible for duties concerning customs, ships, elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, and so forth. All these should be understood as being endowed with the qualities of a minister, as stated in the *Adhyakṣapracāra*: "Those supervisors shall oversee all affairs of other men performing tasks appropriate to their positions: elephant-keepers by the elephant-supervisor, horses and the like by the horse-supervisor, and plowing and so forth by the cattle-supervisor. (7.81)
One should be a worshiper of those brahmins who have returned from the teacher's house;
for this is declared to be the imperishable brahminical treasure of kings. (7.82)

Those who have studied and understood the meaning of the Vedas in the teacher’s household (*gurukula*) and desire to enter the life of a householder (*gārhasthya*) should be honored with wealth; this too is a *naiyyamika* (obligatory) gift. For this very reason, it is said that for kings it is “inexhaustible” (*akṣaya*). Because it is obligatory, it is inexhaustible and lasts as long as one lives. If it were performed for the sake of a specific desire (*kāmya*), it would cease once the fruit has been obtained. That which was stated [in Manu 11.1], “one who seeks to establish a lineage, one who is about to sacrifice,” refers to this very same case.

But others say: in that [other context] giving is prescribed for those who request it, whereas here, because the authority extends even to those who do not request it, the honoring of men must be performed by the mere act of prescription and by the gift of pairs of garments and so forth. Thus it is said: "He should be a worshiper of Brahmins.
It is called a "treasure" (nidhi) because it is like a treasure, due to its yielding the highest fruit. It is "Brahmic" (brāhma) because it is closely associated with Brahman. 8.82.
Neither thieves nor enemies can carry it off, nor does it perish;
therefore, the king should deposit this inexhaustible treasure with the Brahmins. (7.83)

Whatever wealth is given to Brahmins, neither thieves, forest-dwellers, and the like, nor enemies and adversaries, can carry it away. It does not perish through forgetfulness or by being lost as a surety-bond, as might property situated on the ground. (8.83)
It does not spill, it does not perish, and it is never destroyed;
that which is offered into the mouth of a Brahmin is superior to the Agnihotra sacrifices. (7.84)

This very same point, which must necessarily be performed, is stated again by way of another method: that which is offered into the fire sometimes spills—that is, it falls down while being offered—or likewise the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and other items may fall away due to being scorched. Consequently, because of such defects in the ritual, it perishes for the learned (*śiṣṭas*). But this gift given to Brahmins does not possess these faults. For this very reason, he says it is "superior to the *agnihotra*s," meaning superior to offerings made into the fire. Since the word *agnihotra* here functions in its primary sense as the name of a ritual act, the inclusion of the prefix *ā-* must then be explained [as part of the compound]. It means "offered in the mouth. The hand of a Brahmin is indeed his mouth, according to the scriptural statement: "For the twice-born is remembered as having his hand for a mouth" (MDh 4.117). "Superior" (*variṣṭha*) means most excellent. And this is a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*), not a mere censure of the fire-offering itself. (8.84)

A gift given to one who is not a Brahmin yields an equal reward; to one who merely calls himself a Brahmin, it yields a twofold reward; to a teacher, a hundred-thousandfold reward; and to one who has mastered the Vedas, an infinite reward. (7.85)
And "to the Brahmins" is the subject under discussion.

And so it was stated previously: “To a Brāhmaṇa who knows the true meaning of the Veda” (MDh 3.86). Nor is the attainment of the fruit of giving possible according to the literal scriptural statement. For what kind of equality could there be: in terms of genus (*jāti*), quantity (*parimāṇa*), or utility (*upakāra*)? If it were by way of genus, then food given to gods for the purpose of taking medicine would result only in suffering. For medicines are generally bitter, pungent, and astringent; they are purgatives, not producers of pleasure. If, on the other hand, it were by way of quantity, even then, if there were equality of quantity alone regardless of the substance, one might receive copper or some other material such as clay or wood in exchange for gold given in that same measure. If it were by way of both genus and quantity, the aforementioned defects would apply. If it were by way of utility, then too, if the utility were of the same kind—namely, the cessation of disease being the utility of medicine—then in the absence of disease, the fruit would be absent; thus, by means of the gift of medicine which has the cessation of disease as its fruit, a disease would have to be induced. Or else, it would follow that another equally great suffering [is required]. Therefore, this should be viewed in the same way as: “The *nivīta* is for men, the *upavīta* is for the gods; he wears it over the shoulder (*upavyayate*), for he thereby makes it the mark of the gods” (TS 2.5.11.1), where the specific modes of wearing, such as *nivīta*, are not separate sentences from the main injunction. So too should this be understood.

To this it is replied: there is no hearing of a verb here, because all [the words] are equal. In that case, if it were an *arthavāda*, let the phrase "a thousand [for one who has mastered the Vedas]" be the *arthavāda*. If, however, this is an injunction (*vidhi*), then because it cannot be a supplement to another injunction, an injunction must be accepted for every instance, as there is no distinction [between them]. In the case of the *nivīta* and other such [practices], however, because the verb "he wears the sacred thread over the shoulder" (*upavyayate*) is observed there, and because its meaning lacks the fitness to be the object of an injunction, and because singularity is understood, it is rightly considered an *arthavāda*; thus, no specific [injunction] is stated. As for the statement, "There is no giving to non-Brāhmaṇas," that must be forgotten, since giving to the poor, the helpless, and others of all castes is enjoined. And these very sentences are the injunctions regarding the king's giving to Brāhmaṇas.
As for what was stated: "The non-attainment of the fruit as it was heard [is not a fault], because this is accepted in every respect."

To this it is replied: This expression “equal” (*sama*) is a worldly idiom. In common usage, that which is not exceedingly superior is described thus, as in the phrase, “the barley-meal is salty enough. Furthermore, the scriptural mention of the number “twofold” (*dviguṇa*) refers to the expectation of benefit; to whatever extent there is benefit for the recipient, to that same extent the merit becomes twofold. It does not mean the acquisition of that specific substance, nor even a benefit of that same kind, but rather the production of an excellence of joy. Moreover, there is no scriptural mention here of a specific fruit such that one might even entertain the doubt, “Is that very substance to be obtained, or is it that same benefit? When no specific fruit is heard, heaven (*svarga*) is the fruit. Furthermore, in the case of giving sesame seeds and so forth, the attainment of progeny is heard as the fruit. In that context, what room is there for the suspicion of a similarity of substance? Therefore, this is also the meaning: here, through the gift to a progressively superior recipient, the attainment of a progressively superior fruit is established. Thus it has been said: “Indeed, by the distinction of the recipient” (MDh 7.86).

Regarding the term *brāhmaṇabruva*: the word *bruva* denotes contempt. It means one who is a Brāhmaṇa by birth alone, but is devoid of qualities such as Vedic study and so forth. An *ācārya* is one who performs the initiation (*upanayana*). A *vedapāraga* is one who has reached the end of the Veda through both study and hearing. (7.85)
Indeed, depending specifically on the recipient and through faith alone, one enjoys the fruit of giving—whether it be small or great—after death. (7.86)

A *pātra* (worthy recipient) is so called because it causes one to fall away from unrighteous action (*adharmakarman*), or because it protects one who is falling; thus, it is a recipient (*saṃpradāna*). Alternatively, a *pātra* is a vessel for ghee, oil, and the like, and by metaphorical extension (*upacāra*), this [recipient] is also called a *pātra*, for in this case too, a substance is deposited within. And it is said: "This inexhaustible treasure of kings is indeed called the *brāhma* treasure" (MDh 7.82). Its distinction (*viśeṣa*) or difference consists in qualities such as being endowed with virtues or being devoid of them. By that cause, the fruit of giving is obtained—either small or great. What is given to one who possesses qualities, being perfected in conduct and Vedic study (*vṛttasvādhyāyasaṃpanna*), yields much; but what is given to one devoid of qualities yields little. Likewise, it depends upon the degree of faith (*śraddhā*) as well.
Whatever substance, endowed with faith, is given to a worthy recipient according to the rules of place and time— that is the accomplishment of Dharma.

In this context, "place" (*deśa*) refers to a rural region (*jānapada*) other than one's own place of residence. For one who has been exiled to a distant land, the cause of [the merit] being given is the presence [of the recipient]; for one engaged in a sacrifice, it is the deficiency of some component; and [as for] "time" (*kāla*), it is an eclipse of a planet (*graha-uparāga*) and so forth. "Ritual procedure" (*vidhāna*) refers to the excellence of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as the recitation of auspicious verses (*svastivācana*) preceded by the offering of water, as well as the clarity of disposition (*bhāva-prasāda*) and so on. "Substance" (*dravya*) refers to cows, land, gold, and so forth. "Faith" (*śraddhā*) is an excellence of longing for attainment, a continuum of thought (*buddhi-saṃtāna*) such as, "How might this be removed from me?"

Regarding the word *pretya*: this expresses the lack of necessity for the fruit to arise immediately after the action (*kriyā-samanantaram*), but it does not mean that the fruit must belong to a future birth alone; for in the case of Vedic rites, it is understood as a rule that the desire itself is directed toward the fruit [of the action]. (7.86)
But when challenged by those who are equal, superior, or inferior, a king protecting his subjects must not retreat from battle, mindful of the duty of a Kshatriya. (7.87)

When all other means have been exhausted, war is ordained for a king. In that regard, this verse is intended to prohibit indifference on the part of one who has gone to the battlefield and has been challenged, even if his force is equal, inferior, or superior [to the enemy's]. He must not think, "I will not strike because my force is inferior."

Alternatively, if enemies such as forest-dwellers (*āṭavika*) and others, having transgressed the previously established boundaries, invade the territory, or if they enter into an alliance with other enemies against the king, and if they cannot be restrained without war, then one must certainly fight them even if their forces are inferior. Even if they have not been summoned by word, in reality they are indeed summoned.

For this is the duty of Kṣatriyas: when challenged by those of their own kind in battle, they must fight with everyone alike. Birth, age, training, personal prowess, and so forth are not to be taken into account. This duty must be remembered. (7.87)
Not retreating in battles, the protection of subjects, and service to the Brahmins—this is the supreme means for the welfare of kings. (7.88)
This verse is for the purpose of showing that these three qualities have an equal fruit. 7.88.
In battles, kings who desire to slay one another, fighting with their utmost strength and not turning their backs, go to heaven. (7.89)

Where other heroes are summoned for the sake of battle, that is an *āhava*, a conflict. Competing with one another (*mithaḥ*), desiring to kill one another (*anyonyaṃ jighāṃsantaḥ*)—that is, wishing to slay each other—they fight, striking at one another. "With supreme power" (*paraṃ śaktyā*) means according to their full strength; because of Vedic usage (*chāndasatvāt*), the form "param" is used in place of "parayā. The connection is: "fighting without turning their backs, they go to heaven."
But surely, for those who have engaged [in violence] out of greed for sovereignty, since a visible result is possible, how can there be heaven?

It is said: Heaven is contingent upon the rules of warfare to be described by the passage beginning with "not with treacherous weapons" (MDh 7.90), for those rules have no other purpose. Alternatively, even the entry into battle by one who has lost hope because defeat is certain leads only to heaven; for even one who has lost his kingdom may still survive by surrendering to a more powerful foe. Therefore, the possibility of that result [heaven] is appropriate here. Precisely because of this statement, this case does not fall within the scope of the prohibition against suicide. [123]

The rulers of the earth are lords of their realms, not merely their dependents; for their activity is directed solely toward the master’s purpose, not their own. Consequently, how could there be any possibility of fruit for them, being like officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who have been hired for a fee? Likewise, for these [warriors] as well, who are hired for wages, how can there be the production of fruits such as heaven?
But has it not been stated without distinction: "And for one slain in accordance with the duty of a Kṣatriya by weapons raised in battle..."?
"The sacrifice is immediately completed.
(MDh 5.97) Likewise:
"These two persons in the world pierce the solar orb:"

"A wandering mendicant engaged in yoga, and a hero slain while facing the enemy" (PSm 3.30). Likewise, in the *Mahābhārata*, heaven is shown even for those who merely witness the battle. There are also indicative marks in the mantras:
"Those heroes who fight in great battles, those who abandon their bodies..."
Or let him go even to those who give a thousand-fold sacrificial fees.

They demonstrate that for sacrificers who give a thousand-fold dakṣiṇā and for heroes who have surrendered their lives at the forefront of battle, there is great fruit: "Those who fight. And they do not act solely for the sake of death; for at the time of the formal selection (*saṃparigraha*), there is no such agreement as there is in the case of the *hotṛ*, *udgātṛ*, and others, whose selection is specifically for the performance of the priestly duties (*ārtvijya*) defined by their own respective manuals. Therefore, death directed toward the service of a master leads precisely to the aforementioned fruit. Nor is it the case that there is no fruit for another from an action performed by someone else; for indeed, at the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the Aśvamedha, even one who is not the sacrificer—such as the slayer of a Brahmin (*brahmaghna*)—attains purification through bathing.

To this it is replied: In a war for the sake of the subjects, the sacrifice of one's life is indeed for the sake of *dharma*. As for what was stated [in Manu Smṛti 5.97], "by those who have raised their weapons in battle," that refers to one who has been hired for wages and is thus not independent, or to one for whom the equipment has been bound with the thought, "Make ready for the march into battle"; it is with reference to such a person that this statement regarding the sacrificial rite (*yajñasaṃsthā*) is made. And one who is in such a state is "slain while facing the enemy" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.30).

Alternatively, the very absence of hell for one who fights will be his "piercing of the solar orb. Where the territory of another king is struck down, broken, or its people plundered by a king who is the lord of another region, the sacrifice of life in battle for that purpose is for the sake of *dharma*. For hell is indeed blinding darkness; since that [hell] does not exist [for him], there is the statement regarding the "piercing of the solar orb," meaning that he pierces the solar orb, reaches the worlds above, and does not fall downward. For one who has been hired for wages, if war breaks out and he abandons his master, there is a falling into hell; but for one who fights for that purpose and has discharged his debt to his master’s food (*bhartṛpiṇḍa*), being unimpeded by evil deeds and endowed with his own merits, the attainment of heaven and so forth is certain. Therefore it is said: "The sacrifice is immediately completed" (MDh 5.97). This means that without interruption, he attains heaven as the fruit of the sacrifice, according to the general scriptural teaching. Thus, the statement in the *Mahābhārata* regarding the attainment of the fruit of heaven for those hired for wages is also justified. However, the attainment of heaven for those merely watching the battle is merely an *arthavāda* (laudatory exaggeration). Alternatively, when many means of livelihood exist, the fact that one lives by the sword leads to heaven as a matter of rule.

As for the claim that they are not hired for the sake of death: when wages are given to those who bear arms, there is no purpose other than battle, since no specific instruction to the contrary is provided—they are hired with the understanding that "being ready for all tasks, my purpose must be accomplished in every way. Therefore, when battle presents itself, the master's interest must be served even unto the fall of the body; in this way, one becomes free from debt. But if the servant dies when battle has not yet presented itself, then all are indeed free from debt. For while he was engaged in that task, such was his agreement. Furthermore, the observation of indicative marks (liṅga) is also consistent, namely: "At the time of battle, one must fight."

Regarding the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), there is an explicit statement: "Therefore, when they have come together" (MDh 11.82). Here, however, the distinction is that it is accomplished through battle. 7.89.
He now shows those rules whose purpose is invisible:
"While fighting his enemies in battle, he should not strike them with treacherous weapons, nor with barbed ones, nor with poisoned ones, nor with those whose tips are blazing with fire. (7.90)

*Kūṭas*: those which have wooden shafts on the outside but sharp weapons within. *Karṇins*: arrows whose blades are fashioned with ear-shaped plates at the base or in the middle; for once they have entered [the body], they are difficult to extract, and when being pulled out, they tear apart even a part of the body that was not already pierced by the blow. *Digdhas*: smeared with poison. Those whose blades are set ablaze and ignited with fire. One must not fight with these. (7.90)
One should not strike one who has mounted a vehicle, nor a eunuch, nor one with palms joined in reverence;
nor one with disheveled hair, nor one who is seated, nor one who says, "I am yours. (7.91)

One standing in a chariot must strike only one who is mounted on a chariot; one standing on the ground must not be struck. A *klība* is a eunuch or one devoid of manliness. Otherwise, one who is firmly seated—whether sitting on the back of a chariot or on the ground—and says "I am yours," even him one must not kill. The specific wording here is not intended to be restrictive; even if he speaks in a piteous manner with such words as "I am yours" or "I have taken refuge in you," he must not be killed. (7.91)

One should not strike one who is asleep, nor one who is unprepared for battle, nor one who is naked, nor one who is unarmed, nor one who is not exerting himself, nor one who is looking on, nor one who is engaged with another. (7.92)

"Not naked. Or there is the reading "not broken. Since the prohibition concerns one who has abandoned his armor, the case of one who is naked does not even arise [as a subject of the rule]. Therefore, one should be understood as "naked" by virtue of being partially naked due to the absence of a helmet or similar equipment. Also, because one who has turned away from battle is prohibited, even if he stands facing you and says, "I will not fight with you," he must not be pursued; that is, he must certainly be allowed to go. "Not one who is not fighting while looking on": he who is merely a spectator should not be killed. But for one who both looks on and fights, there is no prohibition. "Encountered by another": one who is fighting with another person should not be killed by anyone else. (7.92)

Remembering the dharma of the virtuous, he did not strike one who was suffering from the loss of weapons, nor one who was distressed, nor one who was severely wounded, nor one who was terrified, nor one who had turned away. (7.93)

The calamity of weapons (*āyudhavyasana*) refers to the distress caused by weapons or the breaking of them—such as a sword becoming crooked or the snapping of its bowstring—and so forth; one who has encountered such a situation is meant. One who is "distressed" (*ārta*) is one whose sons, brothers, or others have been slain. Having recognized through the color of the face and other signs that someone is "frightened," even if they are facing the weapon, one should not strike them. One who has "turned back" (*parāvṛtta*) is one who has retreated and stands still. These are the rules. In the view that these are prohibitions, there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) [for violating them]. In that case, the statement regarding the attainment of heaven would be a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). What, then, is the correct interpretation here? It is a prohibition for the sake of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), like the rule "one should not eat *kalañja*. For in this way, the negative particle (*nañ*) functions in its primary sense. Regarding the phrase "the duty of the virtuous" (*satāṃ dharmaṃ*), he says "recollecting" (*anusmaran*) to indicate that this is the conduct of the cultured (*śiṣṭa*). (7.93)
But he who, out of fear, turns his back in battle and is slain by the enemy, takes upon himself whatever evil deed his master has committed. (7.94)

One should not think thus: "If one who has turned away is killed, then he is a wrongdoer; but if he is not killed, he is not. Rather, the statement regarding his fault is based solely on the fact that he turned away. Furthermore, one who has been struck down while turning away should not entertain the thought: "I have experienced the sword-stroke; I am free from debt; I have fulfilled my duty to my master. By showing the extreme gravity of the fault, [the author] demonstrates that such blows serve no purpose for anyone, and thus constitute a grave wrong against the master. As for the statement later regarding the taking over of his merit, that is a mere figurative praise (*arthavāda*). For good or evil performed by one person cannot accrue to another. Nor is there a destruction of merit; rather, it is said that because of the obstruction caused by a great wrong, the fruition of that merit will only manifest after a long period of time. (7.94)
Moreover, whatever merit he has acquired for the sake of the hereafter, the husband takes all of that from one who is killed while retreating. (7.95)

"And whatever merit he has, his master takes it all. [The word] *amutrārtham* means "for the sake of that world. One who possesses wealth (*artha*) is called *artha*; the suffix *-ac* is applied because it belongs to the *arśa-ādi* group. That purpose which was acquired for that world—that is, for the next world—becomes fruitless for him. Alternatively, *amutrārtha* means "his wealth is in that world"; this is a *vyadhikaraṇa* (non-co-referential) *bahuvrīhi* compound, justified by its intelligibility and its functional necessity. (7.95)
Chariots, horses, elephants, parasols, wealth, grain, livestock, women, all kinds of goods, and base metals—whatever one conquers belongs to him. (7.96)

Base metals, beds, seats, copper vessels, and so forth—whatever anyone wins belongs to him. Since it might otherwise follow that these belong to the king by virtue of his sovereignty, this [rule] is stated as an exception to that. Gold, silver, land, dwellings, and so forth belong to the king alone; this enumeration is for that purpose. Weapons, vehicles, and so forth also belong to the king alone. Because grains and other such items are mentioned separately, the word "wealth" (*dhana*) refers here to cattle, buffaloes, and the like; thus they employ the expression, "and half of the royal wealth. (7.96)
"And they shall give a share to the king; such is the Vedic revelation.
And the king must give to all the warriors that which was not won individually. (7.97)

Regarding the principle that "whatever has been won by one should be taken by him," this specific rule is stated: they should give the *uddhāra* (the share) to the king; that is to say, having set aside the best portion of the goods, they should give it [to the king]. They must not take everything for themselves. This is the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), beginning with: "Indra, indeed, having slain Vṛtra... and continuing: "Having become great, he said to the deities, 'Extract for me an *uddhāra*'" (AitB 12.10). Alternatively, in the case of a victory by the king himself, or in a separate victory where no such division exists—such as "this village was won by this man, and this person belongs to another"—where everything has been completely uprooted at once, there the king, according to the maxim of pacifying those who have obtained [booty], should distribute shares among his servants. (7.97)
This eternal warrior-dharma has been declared as unadorned;
a Kṣatriya, slaying his enemies in battle, should not deviate from this dharma.

This is a summary: *yodhāḥ* means warriors; their duty is *yodhadharma*. It is *anupaskṛtaḥ*, meaning unblemished or irreproachable, or alternatively, unaltered. For this very reason, it is called *sanātanaḥ* (eternal). That which is set in motion by one's own whim would be altered (*vikṛta*). He should not deviate nor waver; he should perform it at all times. The mention of the *kṣatriya* is intended to show that he is the primary person entitled to this duty here, and not to imply that for others who might occupy his position, this is not the duty. (7.98)
One should seek to obtain what has not been obtained, guard with effort what has been obtained, increase what has been guarded, and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients. (7.99)

A Kṣatriya should not be content like a Brāhmaṇa; rather, he should exert effort in acquiring what has not yet been obtained. He should protect the wealth he has acquired, increase that which is protected, and build up a treasury. From that, he should give to worthy recipients, and not spend it as this [Brāhmaṇa] does. Thus it is said: "Expenditure should be less than income. (MSSaṃ 5064) || 7.99 ||
One should know that this fourfold [dharma] has human purpose as its aim;
one should perform its constant practice correctly and without indolence. (7.100)

The purpose of those objects that belong to a person is fourfold. For that purpose, these four activities are to be employed: acquisition, protection, increase, and giving. The word *artha* signifies benefit. This purpose exists for the sake of accomplishing the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). One should constantly perform the practice of these four as they arise. (7.100–01)

One should seek what has not been obtained by means of force; one should protect what has been obtained with vigilance; one should increase what has been protected through growth; and one should bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients. (7.101)
He should always have his rod of punishment raised, always display his manly prowess, always keep secret what ought to be concealed, and always seek out the enemy's vulnerabilities. (7.102)

"Udyatadaṇḍa" means one by whom the rod [of punishment] is raised; "udyata" means exerted, that is to say, actively engaged. In this regard, he should constantly discipline the forces of elephants and so forth through training. Instruction should be administered through riding, breaking, and other such methods, as well as through exercises suitable for their performance. The maintenance of equipment such as clothing and ornaments for those mounts constitutes the state of being "udyatadaṇḍa. For one acting in this manner, his possession of the power of energy (*utsāha-śakti*) becomes manifest within the circle of states. Likewise, he should always have his manliness displayed. "Vivṛta" means having come into the light; his duty must be made manifest. At frontier posts, forest stations, and other locations, armored men supervised by trusted agents should be stationed and kept on constant watch. He should always keep his secrets concealed. Having kept what is to be guarded—that which must be hidden—within himself, that place must be made secure through surveillance and protection against the intrigues of others. He should always pursue the enemy's vulnerabilities; having learned the entire faction of the enemy's undertakings, he should immediately sow intrigue therein. (7.102)
The entire world trembles before one who constantly holds his rod of punishment uplifted;
therefore, he should subdue all beings by means of that very rod alone. (7.103)

This is the immediate fruit [of such conduct]: the entire world trembles and fears him, and his majesty becomes renowned. Therefore, a king should subdue all beings—both his own subjects and others—by means of punishment alone. For when he thus exerts himself, his enemies, being terrified, submit without even an effort on his part. (7.103)
One should always conduct oneself with absolute sincerity and never with deceit; being ever well-guarded, one should also recognize the deception employed by the enemy.

*Māyā* is deception; one should not employ it, for in doing so one would become untrustworthy. Furthermore, one should not instigate those of hostile nature whose true character is unknown. One should correctly perceive the deception employed by an enemy, and having understood it through intelligence, one should respond with counter-instigation. In this regard, the faction of those susceptible to instigation (*kṛtyapakṣa*) is fourfold: the angry, the greedy, the fearful, and the insulted.

In this regard, one who has performed some craft or rendered some service may be deceived, won over by favors, or treated with contempt; another who possesses similar skills or services becomes angry, thinking, "His craft or service is not as useful as mine. Such persons are susceptible to incitement. Likewise, one who was previously favored through intimacy, but later fell from honor and office; one whose kinsmen and favorites have been exiled; one who was forcibly honored and taken under one's protection; one who has been excluded by kinsmen; or one whose entire property has been confiscated—such a person, seeing another who possesses equal skill and knowledge being honored while he himself is disregarded, becomes angry, and so forth.

The group of the greedy (*lubdhavarga*) consists of those such as: one who has committed slander and was punished by those of equal fault; those holding all offices of authority whose staffs are wandering within [the palace]; and those who have suddenly accumulated wealth. The group of the fearful (*bhītavarga*) consists of those such as: one who is impoverished, miserly, addicted to vice, and heavily in debt. The group of the humiliated (*avamānitavarga*) consists of those such as: one who is self-conceited; one who has sought honor from an enemy; one who has been struck down by a base person; one who is fierce, reckless, and dissatisfied with his enjoyments.
One should employ this against an enemy and protect oneself with it. 7.104.
An enemy should not discover one's own vulnerability, but one should discover the vulnerability of the enemy;
like a tortoise, one should withdraw one's limbs and guard one's own weak points. 7.105

This very point is stated again: one should exert such extraordinary effort that one seeks out the vulnerabilities of the enemy while protecting one's own. For if someone who is angry or otherwise compromised is discovered by spies such as fraudulent mendicants (*kāpaṭika*) and the like, he will be won over by his own side. "Like a tortoise, one should withdraw one's limbs and guard one's own vulnerability. By this, he expresses that guarding one's own weaknesses against the instigations of others is of great importance. (7.105)
One should contemplate one's goals like a crane, exert prowess like a lion, snatch away like a wolf, and dart away like a hare. (7.106)

Just as a crane, through the application of meditation and other yogic means, employs a stratagem to capture a school of fish—even though they naturally take refuge in difficult waters—by being intent on driving them away; so too, thinking that even objects extremely difficult to attain can be secured through an extraordinary application of reflection upon their purpose, [he proceeds].

One should not fall into despair. Just as a hare, because of its small body, is able to escape even from a pursuing herd, so too a king, though alone and without allies, unable to remain when provoked by enemies rising up on all sides, should escape from that fortress after causing an assault upon the enemy, seeking refuge with one who possesses good qualities. And just as a wolf, intent on seizing livestock, pounces upon them upon finding the keeper's negligence, so too, thinking "he is intent on guarding himself," one must not abandon the effort to seize him; for there will come a time when he will be pounced upon like that wolf. And just as a lion kills even large-bodied creatures such as elephants through his possession of prowess, energy, and power, so too one should not fear a great enemy force; for sometimes even one of little strength, if possessed of energy, slays one of great strength. (7.106)
Thus, while he is victorious, whatever adversaries he may have,
he should bring them all under his control through the expedients beginning with conciliation.

Those who act as adversaries by way of opposition must be brought under control, but not those who act favorably; even they should first be dealt with through conciliation and other means, and not with force from the very outset. (7.107)
But if they should not abide by these [means] through the first three expedients, one should gradually bring them under control by force alone, using punishment. 7.108.

Regarding what was said—that those who cannot be subdued by conciliation and other means should be brought under control by punishment—this refers to that very thing: by means of a gradual application of punishment, having overcome them by force, but not through rashness. (7.108)
Among the four expedients, conciliation and the others, the wise always praise conciliation and force for the constant prosperity of the kingdom. (7.109)

Among the means of policy—conciliation and the others—that are about to be described, conciliation (*sāma*) and force (*daṇḍa*) are praised as being superior. When conciliation is employed, there is no immediate upheaval; through force, however, all objectives are accomplished. (7.109)
Just as a reaper pulls out the weeds while protecting the grain, so should the king protect his kingdom and slay those who stand as obstacles. 7.110

Those who plot against the king—whether they be his friends, kinsmen, or those connected to him through relationship—should not be destroyed, provided they are not involved in the actual act. Only those who are wicked should be punished, not their associates; this is illustrated by the analogy of the reaper. Just as one carefully preserves the grain and removes the weeds when both have grown together and are closely intertwined, so too in one's own kingdom, even between two who are extremely close, only the one who possesses fault should be restrained, not the one who is well-disposed despite being associated with the offender. Therefore, through the discrimination between the virtuous and the non-virtuous, the virtuous are to be cherished and the non-virtuous are to be restrained. (7.110)
The king who, out of delusion and through lack of foresight, oppresses his own kingdom, shall soon be deprived both of his realm and his life, along with his kinsmen. (7.111)

But that king who, failing to exercise the aforementioned discernment, oppresses his own kingdom out of delusion and lack of foresight, shall soon fall from his sovereignty along with his punishments due to the people’s loss of affection and the wrath of his subjects, and even lose his life; he is slain by reckless men acting alone and regardless of their own lives. (7.111)
Just as the vital breaths of living beings waste away from the emaciation of the body, so too do the vital breaths of kings waste away from the emaciation of the kingdom. (7.112)

In his own kingdom, he must generate intense affection through extreme vigilance; for that [kingdom] stands in the place of the body. Just as the life-breaths depart when the body is emaciated by unwholesome food, parching food, and the like, so too do they depart from the emaciation of the kingdom. (7.112)
One should always practice this ordinance for the consolidation of the kingdom;
for a king whose kingdom is well-consolidated prospers in happiness. (7.113)

Gathering [the people] is the method of protection. That king by whom his own kingdom is well gathered through the method of protection—being brought under control or preserved—he prospers in happiness. (7.113)

He should establish a *gulma* (military outpost) within two, three, or five [villages], and likewise he should organize the collection of taxes for hundreds of villages throughout the kingdom. (7.114)

One should establish a *gulma* between two villages. A *gulma* is a troop of men for protection. One should establish a collection (*saṃgraha*) presided over by that very [troop]. One should appoint a man as its supervisor. Here, "collection" refers to the official in charge. This applies likewise to groups of three or five. Alternatively, a "collection" is the place where the king’s revenue is collected. (7.114)
One should appoint a lord of a village, likewise a lord of ten villages,
a ruler of twenty, a ruler of a hundred, and also a lord of a thousand.
One should appoint a lord over each individual village; above him, a lord of ten villages; and so it shall be everywhere. 7.115.
The village headman himself should gradually report any faults that have arisen in the village to the lord of ten villages;
the lord of ten should report them to the lord of twenty.
The lord of twenty should report all of that to the lord of a hundred;
the lord of a hundred villages, in turn, should report it himself to the lord of a thousand.

Those village faults which cannot be remedied by the officer in charge of a single village should be reported to the lord of ten villages (*daśeśa*). In this manner, when unable [to resolve them], it should be notified up to the lord of a thousand (*sahasrapati*). 7.116–17.
Whatever items are to be paid daily by the village dwellers to the king—such as food, drink, fuel, and so forth—the village headman shall receive those. (7.118)

This is the mode of livelihood for one appointed over a village. The village headman (*grāmika*), who is the official in charge of the village, shall receive those [shares]; that is, he should take them for the sake of his livelihood. Grain and other items from the crops, such as the sixth or eighth part, are to be given to the king by the village inhabitants. As he will state: "In grain, the eighth part [is the share] of the sovereign" (MDh 10.120), and so forth. 7.118.
The superintendent of ten shall enjoy the produce of one family; the superintendent of twenty, five families; the superintendent of a village, a village; and the lord of a thousand villages, a city.

One appointed over ten villages is a *daśin*; likewise, one over twenty is a *viṃśin*—this is a Vedic formation of words. A *kula* is a portion of a village, known in some places as a *haṭṭa* and in others as an *uṣṭa*. One appointed over twenty villages is one who has five times that [ten] villages. One who is the superintendent of a hundred villages is the ruler of all. One who is the lord of a thousand is the ruler of a city (*pura*) or a town (*nagara*). "He should assign a livelihood according to the place and the work"—this is the truth. (7.119)
Indeed, another minister of the king— one who is learned, affectionate, and vigilant— should oversee their village affairs as well as their private matters.

Among them, there may arise mutual disagreements regarding village affairs. Therefore, another person—one who is a trusted advisor, highly esteemed, affectionate, and free from passion and hatred—should be appointed to oversee their conduct. (7.120)
And in every city, he should appoint one overseer of all affairs,
stationed in a high place and formidable in appearance, like a planet among the stars.
"High station" means being preeminent. "Of terrible form" means possessing majesty. Like Mars among the stars, he was endowed with a force consisting of elephants, horses, and so forth. (7.121)
He himself should always personally inspect them all;
he should thoroughly ascertain their conduct in the realms through spies.

That city official should patrol all those districts and fill them with his own forces when there is a need. He should thoroughly investigate the conduct of all those district heads and understand it correctly by means of royal spies, such as fraudulent agents (*kāpaṭika*) and others. (7.122)
For the king’s appointed guardians are generally servants who seize the property of others and are deceitful; he should protect these subjects from them. (7.123)

Those whose character is to seize the property of others are "appropriators of others' wealth"; they are deceitful, acting improperly, and are generally persons in positions of authority. Even those who were previously pure protect their own riches; therefore, one should not neglect them on the mere basis of their former purity, but must guard against them with great effort. He should protect these subjects from them. Not only is there a loss of the king's own wealth through such negligence, but they also render the subjects destitute. (7.123)
Those of evil intent who seize wealth solely from litigants, the king shall confiscate their entire property and carry out their banishment. (7.124)

Those appointed as guardians who, for the sake of a mere trifle, punish the subjects by means of litigants, litigators, or officials, the king shall subject them to confiscation of all their property and banishment. (7.124)
He should provide daily maintenance for women engaged in royal service and for servants, according to their rank and their work. (7.125)

He should provide daily maintenance for those women employed in the inner apartments, such as female slaves and others, as well as for the servant class, such as palanquin-bearers and so forth; he should not give a village or a portion thereof once a year. This should be according to their position and work. "Position" refers to the principal appointment, such as guarding the bedchamber and so on; "work" refers to physical labor. Maintenance should be granted in accordance with these. In a high position, even if the work is slight, the maintenance should be large; in a low position, even if the work is great, it should be small—this is what conforms to both. (7.125)
A paṇa shall be the fee for the lowest servant, and six for the highest;
likewise, clothing every six months and one droṇa of grain every month. (7.126)

The *avakṛṣṭa* is one employed in sweeping and cleaning; for his subsistence, a *paṇa* should be given. For the *utkṛṣṭa*, after every six months have passed, clothing for covering should be provided, as well as a monthly measure of grain (*dhānya-droṇa*). A *droṇa* consists of four *āḍhakas*. The author will later state the measurement of a *paṇa* (MDh 8.136). These [provisions] are intended for the purpose of providing a livelihood. 7.126.

Having carefully considered the buying and selling, the distance traveled, the food along with its incidental expenses, and the security of property and person, the king should cause taxes to be paid by the merchants.

The rule for the collection of taxes (*karagrahaṇavidhi*): An examination of purchase and sale such as—"For what price was this bought? What does it fetch when sold? In what length of time is it sold? To what extent is it lost through negligence, or not?"—as well as the distance, whether it can be reached by travel in a long or short time; the basic food, such as parched grain (*saktu*) or boiled rice (*odana*); the incidental expenses (*parivyaya*), such as the utensils for that [food], namely clarified butter, soup, vegetables, and so forth, as well as money and the like; and security (*yogakṣema*), such as the fear of kings, the fear of thieves, or the absence of thieves for one traveling through a forest or a wilderness—it is with regard to these factors that taxes should be levied from merchants. The reading "the king should cause the merchants to pay the taxes" (*vaṇigbhir dāpayet karān*) is more appropriate, because there is no designation of the object (*karmasaṃjñā*) according to Pāṇini 1.4.52 due to the restriction on verbs of motion (*gaty-ādi*) and the like. Alternatively, the verbal root may signify "punishing" (*daṇḍa*); in that case, it possesses two objects (*dvikarmaka*), just like the verb *daṇḍ*. (7.127)
Just as water-creatures, young calves, and bees consume their food little by little, so should the king take from his kingdom an annual tax that is small and small. (7.128)

This is for the purpose that a reduced tax should be collected from those whose cultivation has been exhausted. "Water-dwellers" are leeches; "six-footed" are bees. Just as they become well-nourished by taking only a small amount, so too the king must not practice the cutting off of the roots [of his subjects]. (7.128)
Just as the king and the performer of actions are joined with their fruit,
so should the king, having duly considered this, always apportion taxes within his realm.

He says this very thing: the doer of actions—whether a merchant or a king—should be joined with the fruit; thus he should establish taxes. There is no cause for a fixed limit [of taxation]. Where there is great profit, there more may be taken even beyond the stated limit. (7.129)
The king shall take a fiftieth part of cattle and gold;
an eighth part of grain, or a sixth, or even a twelfth. (7.130)

A fiftieth part should be taken from cattle and gold of high value. Regarding grains, the specific share should be understood in consideration of whether they are easily or difficult to cultivate. *Pañcāśa* means "completing fifty"; in this case, the suffix *tamaṭ* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.56 (*viṃśatyādibhyaḥ*). In the reading *pañcāśadbhāgaḥ*, it is another number, similar to *dvibhāga* and so forth. (7.130)
Furthermore, he may take a sixth part of trees, meat, honey, and clarified butter;
and of perfumes, medicinal herbs, juices, flowers, roots, and fruits.
By the word *druma*, trees are meant; the rest is well known. A sixth part of these [trees] should be taken from the profit. (7.131)
Of leaf-vegetables, grasses, hides, and split-bamboo vessels; of earthenware pots and of everything made of stone.
Even when dying, a king shall not take a tax from a Śrotriya;
nor shall a Śrotriya dwelling in his realm perish from hunger. (7.133)
He should act in such a way that a learned Brahmin does not suffer from hunger within his realm. || 7.133 ||
In whose kingdom a learned master of the Vedas perishes from hunger, his entire realm likewise perishes from hunger before long. (7.134)
This is the fruit of transgressing the immediate injunction. 7.134.
Having ascertained his learning and conduct, the king should provide him with a righteous livelihood;
he should protect him in every way, just as a father protects his own biological son. (7.135)

A righteous mode of livelihood—that by which the duties of the family are not neglected—having established such a livelihood, he should protect it from all sides against thieves and others, as well as from his own excessive expenditure. (7.135)
Whatever dharma he performs daily while being protected by the king, by that the king’s lifespan, wealth, and kingdom increase. (7.136)
This is the fruit of protecting those who follow the Dharma and the sacred tradition: the increase of life-span, wealth, and the kingdom. (7.136)
Whatever little the king may cause to be paid by commoners in his realm who live by trade, even if it is designated as a tax, [he should take] a sixth part of that. (7.137)

One should cause a commoner—other than a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas—who lives by means of occupations such as agriculture, lending money, buying, and selling, to pay a tax. Because the designation "tax" (kara) has arisen for him, he is called "tax-paying" (karasaṃjñita). || 7.137 ||
The lord of the earth should cause artisans, craftsmen, and Śūdras who subsist by their own labor to perform work for one day each month. (7.138)
He may compel those who subsist solely by their craft, as well as Śūdras who support themselves by personal labor—such as porters and the like—to perform work for one day every month. (7.138)
One should not cut off one's own root nor that of others through excessive greed;
for by cutting off one's own root, one afflicts both oneself and them. (7.139)

The non-collection of taxes, duties, and so forth results in the cutting off of one's own root; excessive collection results in the [cutting off of] others' roots. And that occurs through greed; this is a restatement. By the cutting off of one's own root, self-affliction arises due to the depletion of the treasury. Consequently, they too are afflicted. When war has arrived, one whose treasury and power are exhausted will certainly be unable to extricate oneself from being besieged by enemies. That is a great affliction for them. However, one who effects the collection of taxes at all appropriate times does not cause such distress. (7.139)
A lord of the earth should be both stern and mild after considering the task at hand;
indeed, a king who is both stern and mild becomes esteemed.
Sharpness and gentleness must be constantly practiced; such a king becomes esteemed and beloved by his subjects. (7.140)
When exhausted by overseeing the affairs of men, he should appoint to that seat a chief minister who knows the Dharma, is wise, self-controlled, and of noble birth. (7.141)

Weary and weary of observing the affairs pertaining to his subjects, he should appoint a minister endowed with qualities such as knowledge of dharma and who is capable of enduring all burdens to oversee those affairs; however, he should not appoint him to that very throne itself. (7.141)
Having thus performed all these duties incumbent upon himself, he should protect these subjects, remaining both disciplined and vigilant. (7.142)

This is the reflection that "it is thus" upon the meaning already stated, beginning with the gathering of assistants. Having "performed" (vidhāya) what is to be done—that which is beneficial is called "what is to be done"—he should be "engaged," meaning intent upon that; for this very reason, he should be "vigilant. Alternatively, vigilance is the non-lapsing of the intellect at all times. In this manner, he should protect his subjects. (7.142)
He from whose kingdom the subjects are carried off by bandits while they cry out for help—even as he looks on, along with his servants—he is dead and does not truly live. (7.143)

He states the fault in the failure of the two aforementioned forms of vigilance: if he does not remain alert toward the vulnerable points (*gulma-sthāna*) of his realm, then the subjects will be carried off by bandits and thieves who seek out such openings. What can he do for them? Therefore, such a king is as good as dead; his life is itself death. Hence, one must be vigilant. "Wailing" means crying out in lamentation. "They are carried off while he looks on, along with his servants"—this will be seen as a specific indication. Moreover, his own servants merely look on but do not pursue or rescue [the people]; they are all like the dead. (7.143)
The supreme duty of a Kṣatriya is indeed the protection of his subjects;
for a king who enjoys the prescribed fruits of his office is joined with righteousness. (7.144)
The king enjoys the fruit he has obtained; he is joined with righteousness. Otherwise, by performing protection solely for those who favor him, he incurs guilt. 7.144
Having risen during the final watch of the night, purified and composed,
having offered oblations to the fire and honored the Brahmins, he should enter the auspicious assembly hall.

The last watch [of the night] is the *brāhma-muhūrta*. Therefore, it says: "having performed purification, being composed, and having offered oblations into the fire. However, there is no injunction for performing the fire-oblation (*homa*) during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, for at that time the night has four *muhūrtas* remaining. Furthermore, the fire-oblation should be completed when the night has dawned, by avoiding the period of twilight (*uṣaḥ-kalpa*). Having honored and worshipped the Brahmins, he should enter the auspicious and blessed assembly hall. (7.145)
Remaining there, he should bid farewell to all his subjects after greeting them;
and having dismissed all his subjects, he should deliberate together with his ministers.

Remaining there in that assembly hall, he should welcome the subjects who have come for an audience, gladden them with appropriate conversation, glances, rising from his seat, and salutations, and then dismiss them, granting them leave to depart as they came. Then, once they have been dismissed, he should deliberate with his ministers on what ought to be done. The fivefold nature of counsel (*mantra-pañcāṅga*), which consists of the determination of duties pertaining to one's own kingdom and those of foreign kingdoms, will now be shown. (7.146)
Having ascended a mountain ridge or a palace, or having gone to a secluded place, or in a forest free from undergrowth, he should deliberate unobserved. (7.147)

The procedure for the instruction of mantras: Remaining in a secluded place, in a solitary and uninhabited location, one should act so as to remain unobserved, such that people do not know of it even by inference, thinking, “this thing exists. It should be free from *śalākā*. *Śalākā* refers to stalks; a place where there is not even a blade of grass, by which one might suspect, “someone is standing here,” is *niḥśalāka*. These are the constituent factors [of statecraft]: the means of undertaking actions, the excellence of personnel and resources, the division of place and time, the remedy for setbacks, and the successful accomplishment of the task. Alternatively, one should not let the time for petitioning pass, for in that case the counsel would be long-delayed. One should not speak of these matters to others, and the counsel must remain secret. (7.147)
That king whose secret counsel ordinary people do not discover, even when they have gathered together, enjoys the entire earth, even if he is destitute of treasure. (7.148)
This verse is for the purpose of refuting the revelation of mantras: "Ordinary people are those who do not possess mantras and are outside the knowledge of mantras. (7.148)
At the time of reciting the mantra, one should purify those who are dull-witted, mute, blind, or deaf; animals; the very aged; women; barbarians; the diseased; and the deformed. (7.149)

Whatever living being there may be, he should purify them while consulting the mantra; he should remove them from that location out of fear that the mantra might be divulged. Even among animals, such as parrots and mainas, they too can divulge a mantra. Even cows, horses, and the like, when mounted in yoga and having shifted their class (*nikāya*), become carriers of news, whether true or false. Likewise, royal sciences such as those concerning invisibility (*antardhāna*) and so forth are heard of. Since the inclusion of others is already established by the mention of the "defective" (*vyaṅga*)—in the manner of the expression "cattle and bulls"—the specific mention of the others is for this purpose: "In the case of one who is not defective, even if his hands or feet are cut off, one should not have confidence in the observance of the mantra, thinking: 'He cannot go anywhere; he remains confined right here, so how could he divulge the mantras? Alternatively, such persons should not be made mantra-consultants, because of the possibility of mental confusion. Therefore, they are not trustworthy either; hence, one should keep them at a distance. (7.149)
Those who are despised, as well as animals and especially women, betray a secret; therefore, one should be cautious in that regard. (7.150)

Those who are devoid of pride and are held in contempt—such as the low-born and others—might occasionally hear something when there is a lack of respect, or they might sometimes be able to utter syllables; from that, a breach of the mantra would occur. Those who are clever are capable of making some inference regarding the scriptures [from such signs]. (7.150)
At midday or at midnight, being rested and free from fatigue, one should contemplate virtue, pleasure, and wealth—either alone or together with them. (7.151)
One should contemplate the mutual opposition among the factors beginning with dharma; when any one of them increases, it will overcome all the others. (7.151)
The acquisition of those things that are mutually contradictory, the giving away of daughters in marriage, and the protection of sons. || 7.152 ||

The acquisition and gathering of those who possess virtue, wealth, and pleasure, or of ministers; the giving away of daughters in marriage according to the requirements for the accomplishment of one's own purpose; and the protection of the princes—the sons of the king—must be considered. They should be made to accept both dharma and artha through such means as saying, "We are yours. For a new substance, whatever kind of object it is smeared with, soaks up that very thing; likewise, those whose minds are unrefined first grasp whatever is said to them. If they associate with the wicked, then they acquire the nature of those wicked ones. Once they are stained by bad conditioning, they cannot be turned back from calamities. And it is said: "A saffron body-paste cannot be applied to a garment already dyed blue. Therefore, they must be constantly instructed. Among them, those who possess virtues should be promoted; the others should be given a small share. The eldest son, who is highly virtuous and free from envy, should be consecrated as the crown prince (yuvarāja). Thus, one must always be diligent in the protection of the princes. 7.152.
The dispatching of envoys, as well as the remaining tasks to be accomplished, the movements within the inner apartments, and the activities of the secret agents.

He should consider the dispatch of an envoy for the purpose of either making peace or waging war; he should deliberate on matters related to the enterprise already undertaken in order to ensure its stability. Attended by the troops of the *antaḥvaṃśika* (the inner-guard), he should enter the inner apartments (*antaḥpura*). There, he should see the queen only when she has been cleared by elderly women, and never when she is not so cleared. For a brother hiding in the queen’s chamber killed King Bhadrasena; a son hidden within his mother’s bed killed the king of Kārūṣa; a queen killed Vairantya with an anklet smeared with poison, Sauvīra with a girdle, and Vidūratha with a weapon concealed in her braid. Therefore, he should carefully examine these places of confidence. He should prohibit contact between the women of the inner apartments and those with shaven heads, ascetics with matted hair, or sorcerers, as well as with outside female slaves. And he should deliberate upon the activities of spies, such as *kārpaṭakas*, through a succession of secret reports. (7.153)
He [should know] in truth the entire eightfold work and the five groups,
as well as affection and enmity, and the conduct of the circle of states.

Undertaking what has not been done, the performance of what has been undertaken, the excellence of that performance, and the collection of the fruits of action; likewise, conciliation, sowing dissension, bribery, and force—this is the eightfold action.

Alternatively, it consists of trade routes, the construction of waterworks and embankments, the building of fortresses, the maintenance and repair of those already built, the capture of elephants, the digging of mines, the settlement of uninhabited lands, and the clearing of timber forests.
Others, however, say:
In taking up and in casting off, likewise in commanding and in forbidding,
in the fifth [matter], namely in speaking for a purpose, and in the observation of legal procedure.
Constantly engaged in the purification of punishment, the king who possesses these eightfold paths and performs the eight duties goes to heaven, honored by his enemies.

These are the two verses of Auśanas. In this context, "appropriation" (*ādāna*) refers to the collection of taxes. "Distribution" (*visarga*) is the granting of wealth to servants. "Command" (*praiṣa*) is the dismissal of the wicked. "Prohibition" (*niṣedha*) is the restraint of excessive activity by those authorized over state affairs. "Instruction" (*arthavacana*) is the prohibition of improper conduct. "Judicial inspection" (*vyavahārāvekṣaṇa*) concerns cases where there is doubt regarding the specific duties of the social classes (*varṇas*) and stages of life (*āśramas*). It also involves the infliction of punishment upon those who mutually accuse one another and those who have been defeated. Finally, "atonement" (*prāyaścitta*) applies to lapses resulting from negligence; such is the eightfold function [of the king].

The group of five consists of the *kāpaṭika*, the *udāsthita*, the *gṛhapati-vyañjana*, the *vaidehika-vyañjana*, and the *tāpasa-vyañjana*. *Kāpaṭikas* are students who know the secret vulnerabilities of others and are bold. The minister, having won them over with wealth and honor, should say to them: "Taking both the king and me as your authority, whatever is unwholesome must be reported by you at once. An *udāsthita* is one who has fallen away from the religious life (*pravrajyā*). He, being endowed with wisdom and purity, should carry out work on land capable of providing all kinds of food, employing numerous disciples with abundant gold. From the fruits of his agricultural labor, he should provide food, clothing, and shelter for all wandering mendicants (*pravrajita*). Among them, those who desire a livelihood, he should recruit, saying: "In this very manner, the king’s business must be carried out through this profession, and you must present yourselves at the time of receiving rations and wages. All wandering mendicants should then recruit their respective groups. A farmer who has lost his livelihood but is endowed with wisdom and purity is a *gṛhapati-vyañjana*. He should perform agricultural work on the aforementioned land. A merchant who has lost his livelihood but is endowed with wisdom and purity is a *vaidehika-vyañjana*. He should perform trade on the designated land; the rest is the same. One who is shaven-headed or wears matted hair and desires a livelihood is a *tāpasa-vyañjana*. Near the city, surrounded by numerous disciples with matted hair or shaven heads, he should openly eat a handful of vegetables or barley once a month under the pretext of practicing dharma, while secretly consuming food as he pleases. The disciples of this *tāpasa-vyañjana* should honor him with well-known yogic powers. His disciples should predict the acquisition of wealth, and announce: "This fire, this fear of thieves, this execution of the wicked, or news from abroad will happen today or tomorrow; or the king will do this. Then, agents appointed by that secret counselor should bring about those very things for him.

Furthermore, there are secret agents (*sattriṇaḥ*) who must necessarily be maintained by this king, who study the science of marks (*lakṣaṇavidyā*), the science of limbs (*aṅgavidyā*), the science of sorcery (*jaṃbhakavidyā*), the art of illusion (*māyāgata*), the duties of hermitages (*āśramadharma*), and the knowledge of omens (*nimittajñāna*). In that regard, the king should station these five types of persons within his own territory along with these ministers. He should dispatch secret agents under the pretext of being commoners among the ministers, the domestic chaplain, the commander-in-chief, the crown prince, the door-keeper, the inner-apartment attendants, and others—persons skilled in various pretexts, dress, crafts, and languages. Likewise, hunchbacks, dwarfs, Kirātas, the mute, the dull-witted, the deaf, the blind, actors, dancers, singers, and so forth, as well as women who move about in the inner apartments, forest-dwellers in the wilderness, and villagers in the countryside, should be employed for the purpose of male activities, each engaged in their own respective succession of tasks.

These [spies] should be understood by one another as being of such a kind; they are those who move among the enemy and those who move within their own side, those stationed openly and those known to be hidden. Having thus organized the fivefold group for both the enemy and oneself, one should ascertain the loyalty or disloyalty of the ministers, priests, and others through this very fivefold group. In this manner, the movement within the royal circle proceeds: [one must know] which regional ruler is engaged in peace or war, and in what course of action. (7.154)
One should diligently [examine] the conduct of the middle king, the activities of the one seeking conquest, the movements of the neutral king, and those of the enemy. (7.155)

In this circle of kings (*rājamaṇḍala*), these four primary royal elements are principal: the seeker of conquest (*vijigīṣu*), the enemy (*ari*), the middle king (*madhyama*), and the neutral king (*udāsīna*). Among them, that king who is endowed with the constituent elements [of sovereignty] and has risen up [with the thought], "I shall conquer such a world," is the seeker of conquest, by virtue of his possession of the power of energy (*utsāhaśakti*). The enemy is threefold: natural (*sahaja*), ordinary (*prākṛta*), and artificial (*kṛttrima*). The middle king is one situated between the territories of [the enemy and the seeker of conquest]; he is capable of suppressing these two—the enemy and the seeker of conquest—when they are not united, but not when they are united. The neutral king is one capable of suppressing the enemy, the seeker of conquest, and the middle king when they are not united, but not when they are united. (7.155)
In brief, these constituent elements are the root of the circle;
eight others are likewise enumerated, and thus they are traditionally remembered as twelve.

These are remembered. These root-natures (*mūlaprakṛti*) of the circle have been explained; there are eight others as well. For each one of these four natures, there are two natures—namely, a friend and an enemy. These eight, together with the original four, thus become twelve on both sides. (7.156)
The five others are known as ministers, the kingdom, forts, wealth, and the army;
each of these has been described in brief, making seventy-two in total. (7.157)
The five constituent elements, beginning with the ministers, belong to each one of the twelve types [of kings]. Therefore, six times twelve makes seventy-two. (7.157)
Immediately after [the enemy], one should know the ally of the enemy; immediately after the enemy, the friend; and beyond those two, the neutral party. (7.158)

One should know that the enemy is the territory immediately adjacent to the conqueror's land, as well as the enemy's friend and the friend of that friend. Likewise, the territory immediately adjacent to the enemy becomes the friend of the conqueror. The neutral party is beyond those two. Furthermore, the characteristics of enemies and friends should be understood to apply to both natural and artificial relations. (7.158)
He should win over all of them by means of conciliation and other such measures—both individually and collectively—through personal effort and statesmanship. (7.159)

He should reconcile or bring [the enemy] under control. The two human methods are indeed conciliation (*sāma*) and force (*daṇḍa*). Regarding this, it has been said: "They praise conciliation and force" (MDh 7.109). 7.159.
One should always consider the six measures of policy: peace, war, marching, halting, dividing the army, and seeking refuge. (7.160)

In this regard, peace (*saṃdhi*) is for the purpose of mutual benefit through the giving of gold and other gifts; war (*vigraha*) is the opposite of that; marching (*yāna*) is the act of going toward a single goal; staying quiet (*āsana*) is characterized by indifference; duplicity (*dvaidhībhāva*) is the simultaneous adoption of both peace and war; and seeking refuge (*saṃśraya*) is the surrendering of oneself to another. These are the six measures of policy (*guṇas*). Among these, when he considers himself capable of accomplishing such tasks as building fortresses, capturing female elephants, excavating mines, establishing trade routes, felling forests, or reclaiming lands in regions not dependent on rain, and likewise seizing the wealth of his enemy, he should resort to that particular measure of policy which serves to thwart the enemy's intelligence. (7.160)
And this being so:
having examined the task at hand, he should employ sitting encampment, marching, alliance, and war, as well as double-dealing and seeking protection. (7.161)

Having made an alliance with one, one might falsely dispute with another; likewise, having both allied and disputed, one should employ all these actions after having scrutinized the entire situation. There is no fixed time for this. Whenever one deems something appropriate, at that very moment one should act.

If it is impossible to determine a specific time, what is the purpose of the instruction? To this he replies: "It is not possible; the particular is difficult to discern, but the general is easy to discern. This too is useful for the ignorant. (7.161)
A king should know that alliance and war are each of two kinds; likewise, marching and encamping are both twofold, and seeking protection is recorded as being of two types. (7.162)
When the undertaking of the journey is common and likewise the opposite, then that peace treaty, characterized by two features, should be known as one connected with the future. (7.163)

"One who shares the same journey" means: "We two shall go together as equals toward the fruit of the journey, sharing in that fruit equally; you must not disregard me. Whatever is gained from that shall belong to both you and me. Alternatively, one who is the opposite is "one whose journey is not shared," such as saying, "You go elsewhere; I shall go elsewhere. (7.163)

War is said to be of two kinds: that undertaken by oneself for the sake of a specific objective, either out of season or at the proper time, and that waged against a friend who has committed an injury. || 7.164 ||

This is the time for a personal war (*svayaṃ-vigraha*) when one is certainly able to draw out the enemy by means of one's own strength; when one is endowed with enthusiasm; when one’s subjects are united, prosperous, and successful in their own labors such as agriculture; when they will seize those very labors from the enemy; when the enemy’s subjects have lost their livelihood; and when it is possible to win over that enemy’s subjects through instigation. This is the time for a personal war. The opposite of this is the wrong time (*akāla*). In that regard, there is also war for the sake of a friend (*mitrāpakṛte*). If the enemy has harmed that person’s friend, then, having considered that, war should be waged even at an improper time. Even if one is oneself the immediate neighbor of the enemy, nevertheless, with that friend as an ally, it is possible to repel the enemy. The immediate neighbor of the enemy is a friend, whereas the immediate neighbor of the enemy’s territory is the enemy’s enemy.
There is another reading: "and when an injury has been done by a friend. By this, if he (the ally) is oppressed, then war should be waged even at an improper time.

This twofold nature of war is for one's own purpose and for the sake of the friend's purpose. Alternatively, one type arises from one's own advancement, and the second occurs when a friend has been injured and is in distress. (7.164)
When an urgent matter arises by chance, marching alone or in alliance with a friend is said to be the two-fold way of marching. (7.165)

Traveling alone or in a group with a friend constitutes two modes of travel. One should travel alone when one has the capacity; otherwise, one should travel in a group. This is especially so when there is urgent business or when a calamity has befallen another, for at such times one becomes most worthy of being approached. Moreover, if one should ever gain an elevation from another, it is difficult to lose. (7.165)
When one's power has gradually diminished, whether by fate or due to past actions, or out of consideration for a friend—this is remembered as the two-fold state of neutrality (āsana). 7.166.

The posture of waiting (*āsana*) is the self-restraint [of one who has not yet attacked]. That too is twofold: for one who is weakened, by the restoration of strength and treasury; and for one who is prosperous, the consideration of the enemy. Furthermore, the posture of waiting is in accordance with the ally. If the connection between a weakened ally and the enemy is not of such a nature that this [ally] should not be encouraged by his own friend, then one should remain in that state out of compliance with him. And that weakening occurs either by fate or by what was done previously—this is the explanation. Growth and decline of everyone occur for this reason. In this context, "fate" (*daiva*) refers to one's own negligence, a habit of excessive expenditure, and a lack of vigilance regarding one's own forces. "What was done previously" also includes inauspicious karma. Or rather, this may be explained in the reverse order. There is an alternative reading, "out of delusion" (*mohāt*); however, the meaning is already explained by the word "fate. (7.166)

The maintenance of both the army and the sovereign for the sake of accomplishing one's objectives is proclaimed as being of two kinds—namely, *dvaidhībhāva* (duplicity)—by those who know the qualities of the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*). || 7.167 ||

The maintenance of the force and the master should be distinguished: the master of the fort [is supported] by a small force, while the commander-in-chief is joined with a large force elsewhere. Alternatively, some favoring oaths regarding the force should be made in expectation of obtaining gold and other wealth; however, the other [should be supported] more abundantly and swiftly.

This means called *dvaidhībhāva* (duplicity) has this very nature: that it consists in the twofold positioning of both the power and the master. In this regard, another form of duplicity of such a kind must be stated; yet nothing of that is expressed by this [definition]. This is merely the twofold positioning of power and master. In that context, it should be said: duplicity exists within *māyā*, and this is its twofold nature.

It is said: this is to be understood through the force of the context; it must be performed for the sake of favoring others and for the sake of one's own purpose. This is the twofold division of the state of being two-fold. 7.167.
Seeking refuge with the virtuous for the sake of accomplishing one's goals when oppressed by enemies is recorded as being of two kinds. (7.168)

Seeking refuge elsewhere for the sake of securing one's resources while being oppressed by enemies: when one's wealth is under threat, its cessation constitutes "wealth" (*artha*); for the sake of securing that [cessation], one may resort to another who is capable, leaving one's own country and going there. Furthermore, seeking refuge for the sake of a pretext (*vyapadeśa*), even when not currently oppressed: in order to avoid future oppression, one may resort to another for the purpose of creating a pretext. By means of this, the success of the pretext is ensured through the thought, "This person is his ally; he cannot be oppressed. Thus, "seeking refuge for the purpose of a pretext" is expressed by the word *vyapadeśa* through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
There is an alternative reading: "for the sake of designation.

But where, then, should one seek refuge? To this he says: "among the virtuous. One should take refuge with any one of those kings who are virtuous, from whom no treacherous conduct is to be feared. By the word "virtuous" (sādhu), qualities such as the capacity to protect from humiliation and so forth are indicated. (7.168)
When one perceives that one's own future will certainly be superior, while the present suffering is slight, then one should resort to peace. (7.169)

The future (*āyati*) is the time yet to come.
