If he should think: "This [rival] is equal in strength to me, or perhaps even weaker; however, by means of instigation once the right time has arrived, or through the winning over of allies, I am able to overcome him," then he should make a treaty. *Ādhikya* is the state of possessing superior strength. *Dhruvam* means certain. *Tadātve* refers to the present time. (7.169)
When he considers all his subjects to be exceedingly well-pleased, and likewise himself to be highly exalted, then he should wage war. (7.170)

He should consider his own subjects, such as the ministers and others, to be joyful, endowed with enthusiasm and loyalty, and won over by gifts and honors; he should regard himself as preeminent due to the abundance of his treasury, elephants, horses, and so forth. Then, under some pretext, having caused a breach in the peace treaty, he should resort to war. (7.170)
When he perceives his own army to be joyful and well-nourished in spirit, and that of the enemy to be the opposite, then he should march against the foe. (7.171)

*Bhāva* (prosperity) is the cause for nourishing joy. Being well-distributed with abundant wealth, and the fact that their agricultural and other labors have borne fruit—these and similar factors are the causes for joy and prosperity. *Bala* (power) consists of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. When these are in a state contrary to those of the enemy, then one should march against the foe; the meaning is that one should lead an expedition against the enemy. It is not only the causes for conflict that are the causes for marching; rather, those [causes] as well as the decline of the enemy's joy and prosperity and of his constituent elements (*prakṛtis*) [are the causes]. (7.171)
But when he is completely depleted of both mounts and troops, then he should sit with diligence, gradually conciliating his enemies. (7.172)

"Vāhana" refers to elephants, horses, and chariots; "bala" refers to infantry. The distinction between these two is like that between "cattle" (go) and "bull" (balīvarda). When his own force is depleted, he should remain seated while conciliating the enemy. Conciliation (*sāntvana*) consists of winning over [the enemy] through both diplomacy (*sāman*) and the bestowing of gifts (*upapradāna*). (7.172)
When the king considers his enemy to be stronger in every respect, then, having divided his army into two parts, he should accomplish his own purpose. (7.173)

It is impossible for one who is besieged by a powerful force to maintain a reconciliation; therefore, taking refuge in a fortress is beneficial. Furthermore, establishing a fortress is itself a form of double-strategy (*dvaidhībhāva*), as has been explained previously. For it is observed that even a more powerful king, when in calamity, divides his forces into two parts. (7.173)
But when he becomes most vulnerable to the forces of the enemy, then he should quickly seek refuge with a righteous and powerful king. (7.174)

When one thinks, "I am most easily assailable, most easily overcome, and situated in a fortress," then one should quickly abandon that fortress and seek refuge with another who is righteous, such that no treachery is to be feared and whose nature is stable and composed of glory. By the word "powerful" (balin), this is clearly demonstrated. (7.174)
One should always serve with every effort that man who subdues both the subjects and the enemy's forces, just as one would serve a teacher. 7.175

It has been stated that [the king] must be powerful. To explain by how much power one becomes powerful, this is said: he who is capable of subduing both the king's wicked subjects and his enemies should be relied upon. He should be served like a teacher, having abandoned pride. One should not think, "This man is merely a peer of the Great King and can be treated with equality. He should be served like a master, through every effort and means, with pleasant words, and by remaining in his presence at the appropriate time. (7.175)
If he should perceive even there a fault arising from seeking refuge, he should nevertheless engage in fair combat without hesitation. (7.176)

If, even in that very refuge, one should perceive or somehow recognize a fault caused by that reliance— namely, the signs of perceiving such faults: regret after giving, disparaging the previously performed sacrifice, recounting his misdeeds, withholding one's gaze, and speaking with hostility— these are the behaviors of a wicked person.

Then, when even that recourse is understood to be productive of harm—the word "even" implying that it is not the case that there is no faultless recourse—one should, remaining unperturbed, engage in fair combat even at such a time. For ruin does not necessarily follow from seeking refuge; indeed, one is seen to be defeated by a weak opponent despite possessing great strength. Moreover, in the final extremity, there is merit in either outcome: in victory, sovereignty; in defeat, certain heaven. We shall demonstrate the excellence of battle later. One who possesses the power should march for the conquest of the circle of states by relying on each individual quality [of the six measures]. (7.176)
A king who understands policy should employ every means such that his allies, neutrals, and enemies do not become superior to him. (7.177)

"By means of expedients" refers to conciliation (*sāman*) and the other methods, either individually or collectively. "By all [means]" implies that one may employ even stratagems such as making peace (*saṃdhi*) when necessary. "In that manner" means one should strive by whatever method is appropriate. A "king who knows policy" is one who understands the *Arthaśāstra*, possesses innate wisdom, or is skilled in statesmanship (*naya*) and the like. He should ensure that his three powers (*śakti*) do not fall short of those of his allies and others; likewise, in the administration of affairs concerning the constituent elements of sovereignty (*prakṛti*) and so forth, he should make himself superior to them. The mention of the "middling" enemy is omitted here for the sake of metrical requirements, yet he too must be taken into account and not neglected under the pretext of being a friend. For there is no such thing as a "friend" apart from one's own interests. A friend is defined by a fixed relationship; however, one who has attained superiority, or who turns toward self-interest, becomes an enemy even if previously a friend. As Vyāsa said:

"No one is anyone's friend, nor is anyone anyone's enemy; friends and enemies are to be understood according to the application of circumstances. (MBh 12.136.104) "Thus, by these means, one should deliberate upon the circle [of states]. (7.177)
One should examine the future state of all undertakings as well as their present condition, and one should also truly discern the merits and defects of all past actions. (7.178)

"Tasks" (*kāryāṇi*) refers to actions and purposes. One should investigate all of these as they are about to be undertaken: their "future" (*āyati*), which is the subsequent period of their development; and their "present" (*tadātva*), which is the state of their commencement during the current time. This investigation should be conducted "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*), for tasks have many facets and can change in an instant. In this regard, the instruction for investigating is intended to answer the question: "How should one undertake those tasks for which neither of the two times [past and future] is pure? Furthermore, one should investigate in reality the merits and faults of all past and transcended actions. Here too, having investigated the merits and faults of the past, the purpose of the instruction to investigate the reality of the merits and faults of past actions is to consider how one might indeed undertake again those very actions that were meritorious in the past. (7.178)
One who knows the merits and defects of the future, who makes swift decisions in the present, and who understands the consequences of past actions is not overcome by enemies. (7.179)

For he who thus understands the merits and defects of actions in the future, that is, in a time yet to come, is necessarily one who acts with deliberation; he undertakes [the task] himself and does not incur fault. Such is the purpose of knowledge. He who quickly ascertains what is present in the current moment does not delay in action; being one who reaches a quick decision in the present, he acts swiftly, performing what is meritorious and not what is faulty. When an action has been performed in the past, he who understands the action from its conclusion—that is, he who does not fail to complete it—becomes superior due to his connection with the fruits of all meritorious actions and will not be overcome by enemies. Indeed, it is not possible to provide a full instruction on the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) in the treatises on Dharma; therefore, only a mere indication has been given. (7.179)
He should arrange everything in such a way that his friends, neutrals, and enemies do not gain the upper hand over him; this is the summary of political strategy.

One should act in such a way that they do not conspire through various means, using either those [already mentioned] or other acquired methods; this is the concise principle, which is the summary of the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*). Furthermore, in this way, there is no contradiction regarding deception. This should be understood as follows: by guarding against instigation (*upajāpa*) regarding tasks to be done, by providing remedies for calamities, by maintaining control over one's own circle (*maṇḍala*), and by the correct application of the qualities and means, there is success in undertakings. (7.180)
Now he describes the action of one about to march forth:
"But when the lord sets out upon his expedition toward the enemy's kingdom, then he should proceed slowly toward the enemy's city according to this rule. (7.181)

When he intends to attack the enemy's kingdom by marching directly against it, he should proceed according to this method without haste. The introduction of what is about to be said is for the sake of easy understanding. (7.181)
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the lord of the earth should set out on his journey;
or else, according to his strength, he may do so toward the months of Phālguna or Caitra.

Desiring to wage war for a long duration, depending on the enemy to be attacked and his own strength, one who possesses superior forces should march against the enemy's kingdom—abounding in autumn and spring crops—in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa. For by marching then, he easily secures the autumn harvest already stored in houses and other places, brings in the spring crops, and his desire is great, being capable of accomplishing tasks such as besieging forts; furthermore, the roads are not filled with well-known detours, marshes, water, or creepers; the season is neither too hot nor too cold; and even though the crops have been gathered, they are not yet fully utilized, as the enemy, considering the delay in destroying the three types of crops, seeks refuge elsewhere. Thus, the destruction and depletion of both harvests is properly accomplished, while his own forces suffer no decline. If, however, the objective is merely to cause damage, or if the enemy country and so forth can be dealt with in a short time, one who possesses superior forces should march in the months of Phālguna or Caitra against a region abounding in spring crops. At that time, his own fodder and other supplies are available, due to the destruction of the enemy's crops located in the fields. "According to his strength" means that he should march in whatever manner is appropriate to his military power. (7.182)
The exception to this is as follows:
"But even at other times, when he perceives certain victory, he should march forth after declaring war, or when a calamity has arisen for the enemy. (7.183)

Apart from this, one may also march during other seasons such as the rainy season; whenever one considers victory to be certain for oneself, then one should march. For when the army consists primarily of elephants and horses, and the cavalry and elephant forces are at their peak during the rains, then victory is absolute due to the power of one's own troops and the favorable season. "Calamity" refers to a state of distress involving the enemy's own troops, treasury, and so forth. When that has arisen, one should march regardless of whether it is one's own troops' time or season. For an enemy afflicted by calamity is easily subdued; like a piece of wood, he perishes merely through the application of a rope (guṇa). "Having declared war" means one should march after having seized and challenged the one who is to be attacked. In this very case, "greatness" is understood. (7.183)
Having performed the ritual arrangements at the base according to the rules, as well as the preparations for the journey, and having secured his residence and properly stationed his spies; 7.184.

At the base, in one’s own fort and kingdom, one should act; furthermore, regarding the rear-enemy (*pārṣṇigrāha*), having made provisions and counter-measures there, one should first make the fort well-equipped with abundant grain and so forth, as well as machines, walls, and moats. For the kingdom as well, one should provide protection for one’s own forces from the guild-armies (*śreṇībala*). Having restrained those who are prone to giving or bribing, they should be stationed at the frontiers. Regarding the rear-enemy, he says: a capable portion of the army should be stationed within one’s own kingdom. The equipment for the expedition—suitable for elephants, horses, and other forces, such as weapons and armor—should be ready. Having given instructions to others according to the rule. "Base" means a firm foundation. What then? One should observe those belonging to others who are angry and so forth; having won them over and brought them under control, and having properly and accurately arranged for the knowledge of the enemy's intentions once the siege has ceased in the foreign territory, one should employ them. Whether this person has begun to gather visible resources, or intends to incite the circle of enemies, or to seek refuge with the middle king or the neutral king, or whether he desires to seize the root-expedition or to effect a strategic cut-off according to the rule—it is in accordance with these circumstances that one should act. (7.184)
Having cleared the threefold path and his own sixfold power,
he should march toward the enemy's city according to the rules for a campaign against an opponent.

There are three kinds of roads: the *jāṅgala* (open), the *ātapta* (exposed), and the *āṭavika* (forest). Some say there are three kinds by substituting "forest" (*vana*) for "wilderness" (*āṭavika*). Others say they are the elevated, the depressed, and the level. Having thus cleared the three types [of terrain], one should cut down trees, shrubs, and creepers that obstruct the path, level the high and low ground, create fords across rivers and ravines, eliminate predators that block the way, win over those who incite [enemies], and ensure the availability of fodder, fuel, and other necessities. Regarding the "sixfold army": some say the sixfold army consists of elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, the treasury, and laborers. Others substitute "transportation" (*prakṣepaṇa*) for the treasury. Still others [classify it] according to the distinction between hereditary troops (*maula*), hired troops (*bhṛtya*), guilds (*śreṇi*), allies (*mitra*), enemies (*amitra*), and forest tribes (*āṭavika*). By means of preparations for war (*sāṃparāyika-vidhāna*): "War" (*saṃparāya*) refers to the hardship encountered in battle; that which has this as its purpose is "for the sake of war. Alternatively, one may march against the enemy using fortification techniques. This includes the encampment of the army in various locations, establishing fixed and mobile defensive lines, and constructing walls with many openings, enclosures, planks, and branches, and so forth. However, these measures are especially required when one has set out on a military expedition. (7.185)
One should be especially vigilant toward a friend who serves the enemy and one who is hidden;
likewise, toward one who has gone and returned, for such a person is a foe intent on causing hardship.

One should be more cautious regarding a secret, hidden enemy who has served the foe, as well as one who has gone and returned; one should be more diligent and more attentive toward them, meaning that one should not trust them. For such a person is a more dangerous enemy than others, such as those who are merely angry. Thus, from the expressions "more cautious" (*yuktatara*) and "more dangerous" (*kaṣṭatara*), it is understood that one who has gone and returned is not to be accepted by anyone else. He is of four kinds: 1. One who has gone for a specific reason and returns for the opposite reason—for example, having left due to a fault, he returns again after abandoning both faults and virtues. 2. One who has come for a reason—he should be abandoned because of his fickle intellect and the fact that he does anything at random; no further confidence should be placed in him. 3. One who has gone for a reason and come for a reason—for example, having left due to a fault of his master, he comes back from another due to his own fault; he should be honored if he has returned out of attachment, and then he may be accepted. 4. One who is instigated by the enemy, or who wishes to cause harm because of that same fault; in that case, he is not to be accepted. (7.186)
Setting out against a foreign kingdom,

he should march along that route in either the staff-array (*daṇḍavyūha*), or the wagon-array (*śakaṭavyūha*), or the boar-array (*varāhavyūha*), the crocodile-array (*makaravyūha*), the needle-array (*sūcīvyūha*), or the eagle-array (*garuḍavyūha*). (7.187)

In this context, an array (vyūha) shaped like a staff is a *daṇḍavyūha*. Similarly, it should be applied that an array in the shape of a cart is a *śakaṭavyūha*, and so forth. With the commander-in-chief (*balādhyakṣa*) in front, the king in the middle, and the general (*senāpati*) in the rear; with elephants on the flanks, horses near them, and infantry behind them—this compact formation on all sides is the *daṇḍavyūha*, which is not horizontal and is to be employed when there is danger from all directions. The *sūcīvyūha* is for troops emerging from a position on level ground; it has heroic men at its head, is extremely long and vertical, and thus advances against the enemy's flank while remaining equal to others. The *makaravyūha*, however, is broad at the mouth and the two rear parts (the "tail"), by which it is praised; it does not allow the entire weak force to be caught, nor does it lose its purpose. For when it is struck by the heroes, it causes the breaking of even the others. One should certainly hold its end, which is restricted for other purposes. As for the remaining force, one should insert it within the array. Thus, according to the specific formations mentioned or in view of the stated purposes, one should march on level ground using the *daṇḍa*, *garuḍa*, and *sūcī* arrays; on uneven or narrow ground, one should use the *śakaṭa*, *makara*, and *varāha* arrays. (7.187)
From whichever direction he anticipates danger, toward that side he should extend his forces;
and he himself should always take up his position in the lotus array.

On that route, from whichever place there might be apprehension of danger from those who act as enemies, he should extend the army from his previous encampment through that region for the distance of a *gavyūti* or more. There, the forces of infantry, cavalry, chariot-riders, and elephants—well-supplied with fodder, firm in their striking power, extensive, nourished by the enemy's own resources, and mutually supporting one another—should remain alert and held in check. Forming a circular array spread out on all sides with the conqueror stationed in the center, this is the *padmavyūha*. In this manner, he should always encamp when leaving a city or a village. (7.188)
The commander-in-chief and the army supervisor should station themselves in all directions;
and from whichever direction he fears danger, that he should designate as the east.

The general (*senāpati*) is the lord of the entire wealth and the superintendent of the army; since those two do not exist in multiple copies and because they are designated by a dual number, it is impossible for them to be present in all directions. Therefore, their subordinates are referred to by that term. Because of the arrangement of their respective men, those two [the general and the superintendent] are effectively stationed in all directions. Thus, having deployed various horses, elephants, and so forth, along with those stationed in connection with them, on all sides for the purpose of battle, and having placed a mountain, a forest, or a pit behind as a protector, one should arrange the camp facing whichever direction one fears danger might come from—just as the wise would do for the sake of an exit facing forward. (7.189)
And he should station trusted men as outposts on all sides—men who are skilled in both their positions and in combat, fearless and unwavering. (7.190)

He should station many *gulmas* (detachments) consisting of human groups. Some should be positioned directly all around with conchs and drums, others otherwise. And what arises therein is difficult to cure and leads to great misfortune. He distinguishes them by their qualities. "Trustworthy" (*āpta*) means those similar to the trustworthy, for the sake of non-distinction. "Those who have made a signal" (*kṛtasaṃjñān*): those by whom a signal has been made for the purpose of communication; they are "those who have made a signal. At the opportune moment in battles, by means of sounds of conchs, kettledrums, banners, and other musical instruments, we shall indeed raise the war-cry (*tūrya*); and when there is fear of their retreat, one should act in this very way. When the conch is sounded or the banner raised, one must stand separately, [or] thus united, thus strike, thus turn back, and so forth—this is the established rule. "Skilled in position" (*sthāne kuśalāḥ*): others, being brave, may come together; in this [position], we are not separate while the enemies are separate, and so forth. They are skilled in following during battle and the like; having entered after making a wide advance with united forces, those striking from the rear should be employed in a varied manner, and the rear of the broken enemy, who have fled by hundreds of different paths, should be seized, and so forth. "Fearless" (*abhīravaḥ*): by this, they are shown to be extensive and united. "Unwavering" (*avikāriṇaḥ*): those joined with others who are of an undivided nature. Thus, he should station these *gulmas* all around in the three directions, covering a distance of one *gavyūti*, numerous and with no fixed location day by day. He should remain vigilant for the purpose of awakening fear. The people become confident through gifts, honors, the display of tasks, and so forth. When the battle is concluded, the battle is for the self-interest of everyone along with the ministers and others, thinking: "I am king in name only," "We are all for the sake of equal wealth and enjoyment," or "In victory there is the kingdom, in defeat there is heaven"—for these reasons they have come. (7.190)
One should make a small number of troops fight in close formation, while one may at will spread out a large number;
having arrayed them in the needle or the thunderbolt formation, one should cause them to fight.

For when a large and extensive force encounters a powerful enemy, it perishes by being broken down limb by limb through the impact of vehicles; and since these [individual soldiers] are produced for that destruction, one should instead fight with a small number of one's own men who are united. Fighting while looking out for one another, striking at each other, through mutual assistance, mutual affection, and rivalry, they become capable of withstanding a united enemy. One may think: "Let me, for the sake of the task, spread them out as much as desired and fight them scattered," and so forth; but if they are divided, fear will come upon them, as there would be terror upon seeing many enemies or even many of their own. The *sūcī* (needle) is a previously mentioned variety of the *akṣa* array, arranged three-fold—front, back, and sides—and used for breaking through [the enemy]. Having thus divided oneself into a *sūcī* array, one should fight. Because they are capable of establishing and deploying all the arrays of the virtuous, they are indeed accepted for this reason. However, when these two [arrays] belong to the enemy's force, then the opposite should be done regarding one's own force. But when they are equal, [one should choose based on] being well-nourished, loyal, skilled, honored, numerous, and acting toward a single goal; thus, according to the specific circumstances, one should act as possible. From the statement "one should fight," it follows that the king himself, for the purpose of coordinating that [force], should remain as a support within the array, the fort, or other such positions. As it is said in the *Samānatantre*:

Having advanced two hundred bow-lengths, the king should remain as a reserve; however, for the purpose of rallying broken troops, he should not fight without being a reserve. (Kautilya’s Arthaśāstra 10.5.58) 7.191.
One should fight with chariots and horses on level ground, with boats on marshy land, and likewise with elephants;
one should fight with bows in places covered by trees and shrubs, and with swords, shields, and other weapons on firm ground.

He speaks for the purpose of arranging the deployment of armies in various regions: one should fight with chariots and horses on level ground, for there they encounter no obstruction. A marshy region (*anūpa*) is one abounding in water; even there, one should fight with elephants where the water is shallow, but with boats where it is deep, for they can move easily there. In a place covered with trees and shrubs, one should fight with bows; by the mention of these, places cluttered with bullocks, pits, and the like are included, because their effect is the same. "High ground" (*sthala*) refers to a region free from stones, trees, creepers, pits, and so forth; success is achieved therein. One should fight with handheld weapons such as arrows and missiles such as spears, because of the nature of close-quarters combat. This is stated for the purpose of demonstrating the appropriate application of these means. (7.192)
Furthermore:
He should station the Kaurukṣetras, the Matsyas, the Pañcālas, and those born in Śūrasena—men both tall and short—at the vanguard of the ranks. (7.193)

Kurukṣetra is well known. Matsya is the region of Virāṭa. In Nāgapura are both Pañcālas; likewise those from Kānyakubja and Āhicchatra. The Śūrasenas are those born in Mathurā. In some instances here, the suffix indicating the abstract state (*bhāvārtha*) is indicated as elided. For those born in these regions are generally large-bodied, powerful, broad-chested, brave, proud, and difficult to withstand—those who, stationed at the front, become causes of fear for their enemies. Those with long bodies, even when stationed in small areas, produce long-drawn breaths due to their great stature. But those who are light [of build], being unable to endure death, strike while hidden by fearless people, yet they are incapable of causing harm. And these others serve as mirrors for them. (7.193)
Having arrayed his forces, he should gladden them and examine them thoroughly;
he should also discern the movements of the enemies even as they are fighting. (7.194)

Having arranged his battle formation (*vyūha*) and displaying his own army vigorously, he should inspire them with joy, saying: "What is there for these [enemies] to conquer? They are already conquered by your valor! He should also provide occasional instruction on the omens, saying: "In victory there is great gain of wealth and happiness for those directly and indirectly dependent on you; in death as well, there is heaven and the repayment of the master's wages; in defeat, all three are absent. He should say: "Respect such fixed omens; let there be a display of force. If the principal man is a relative, or if the king remains under the pretext of not accepting [the challenge] due to cowardice and does not personally desire the fight," and so forth. In that regard, those who might say: "This is not so. This slaughter here is for our own sake; for us who live by the sword, this is the specific duty of battle, an imperishable state, and the exertion of one’s own dharma. The king, who is the cause of misfortune, must be protected in every way. He remains here for the purpose of granting favor—rest to us who are exhausted and happiness to those not yet exhausted,"—these he should specifically seize. Whether they cause the victor to boast or effect the destruction of the enemy, he should bring them under control through conciliatory means, such as embraces, gifts of ornaments, and the like. And he should observe the behavior of the enemies as they fight: how they act in battle, whether their treasury or their strength is depleted; whether some are double-minded or others are resolved on one side. Because of the constant uncertainty of human nature—even those who assist may do so out of self-interest—he should place the wicked among the strength of trusted men. (7.194)
Just as an enemy takes refuge in a fortress, [the king] states the means for seizing that fortress:
"Having besieged the enemy, he should remain encamped and harass his kingdom;
he should constantly corrupt his supplies of fodder, food, water, and fuel. (7.195)

A siege should be conducted in such a manner that no one may exit nor anything enter. "The kingdom" refers to the territory outside the fort. Its "affliction" consists of the destruction of its own local supplies by means of flooding and so forth. The "spoiling" or destruction of fodder and other provisions is achieved by mixing them with harmful substances and the like. (7.195)
He should break down tanks as well as walls and moats;
he should launch a sudden assault upon him at night and likewise cause terror. (7.196)

The mention of "tanks" (taḍāga) is intended to represent all types of water reservoirs. In that regard, the purpose regarding a tank is to breach it by means of a dam. A rampart is to be breached by engines or destroyed by means of a tunnel. A moat is to be dealt with by filling it or by breaking its banks. One should launch an assault through breaches using elite warriors. At night, one should cause terror within the fort by means of men carrying jars of fire on their heads and making the cries of jackals. Those men who, having personally observed portents, remain awake at night—since the population, exhausted from staying awake, becomes easy to overcome. (7.196)

And at that time, he should repeatedly instigate those who can be won over, and he should ensure that this is understood; when fate is favorable, he should fight, free from fear and desiring victory. (7.197)

Those who should be sown with dissension (*upajapyāḥ*) are the enemies' angry subjects, those of noble birth, and those desiring their own kingdom; the reason for this is that one should sow dissension among them. The meaning of "one should sow dissension" (*upajaped*) is that one should cause the agent to be designated as the one to be acted upon. The meaning of "one should sow dissension" is that one should cause [the enemy] to accept [the proposal]. *Upajāpa* (sowing dissension) consists of causing a separation from [the enemy's] support and inducing them to practice what is beneficial to themselves. By means of that, one should perceive whatever good deed has been performed by the enemy—even if he is stationed in a fort—such as the commencement of some action intended to provoke the forest-dwellers (*āṭavika*), the rear-attackers (*pārṣṇigrāha*), and so forth, or an alliance with either the middle king (*madhyama*) or the neutral king (*udāsīna*). And when fate is favorable—that is, when the fortune of the seeker of victory (*vijigīṣu*) is propitious—when the constellations, planets, divine omens, and auspicious moments are conducive, and when dreams seen and other signs are favorable, and when the winds and other elements are blowing in a favorable direction, then desiring victory and free from fear, he should first go out from his fortifications to fight. (7.197)
One should strive to conquer the enemy through conciliation, bribery, or sowing dissension—either collectively or individually—and never by means of war. (7.198)

One should not fight impulsively. First, there is the instruction for establishing a distinguished position and being well-disposed toward one another, including sitting together, conversing, and seeing each other’s wives [275]. The "bestowing of gifts" [276] refers to the presentation of wealth such as gold and so forth for the purpose of generating affection. "Sowing dissension" is the winning over of those belonging to the enemy's family and so forth. Furthermore, through such distinctions, there is no cause for alarm or fear therein; thus it is said. (7.198)
Since victory is seen to be uncertain for two who fight, and defeat likewise in battle, one should therefore avoid war. (7.199)
For this rule is not observed: that whoever wins is necessarily extremely strong, and therefore whoever is defeated is necessarily extremely weak; thus, victory is uncertain. 7.199
When even the three previously mentioned expedients are unavailable, one who is well-prepared should fight in such a way that he conquers his enemies. (7.200)

Even when the outcome of conciliation and the other [stratagems] is uncertain and victory is equally possible for both sides, how much more so should one fight in such a manner—along with the proper form—that one’s own victory may be secured? For in victory there is a kingdom, and even in death there is heaven; thus, in either case, there is victory. The plotting of obstacles against the enemy through methods such as treacherous warfare (*kūṭayuddha*) must be avoided immediately, as they involve extreme destruction and oppression. Thus Vyāsa said: “For those who return [to battle] and for those who have lost all hope for life... (MBh 12.100.13).
O Dhanañjaya, even Śakra himself would not be able to stand before him.
When defeat is certain, then it is proper to withdraw; for once life has departed, one does not accomplish any purpose by which one might behold auspicious things or attain heaven when dead. (7.200)
Having conquered, he should worship the gods and the righteous Brahmins;
he should grant exemptions and proclaim amnesties of safety.

Having conquered the enemy by whatever means possible, this [kingdom] has attained tranquility. Therefore, in this city and its countryside, he should honor the righteous gods and Brahmins—who perform their prescribed duties according to their capacity—by offering incense, perfumes, flowers, and other substances, avoiding what is forbidden, and acting with self-restraint as desired, through the performance of rites such as distribution and the clapping of hands, honoring each according to their merit. For the sake of exempting the householders, he should grant them a fixed status by providing specific tax exemptions (*karabhāra*), tolls (*śulka*), and land grants, or by granting them a portion of the revenue for one or two years. Furthermore, he should proclaim to the high-ranking citizens and country-folk by the beating of drums and the striking of maces: "Let those who, out of devotion to their sovereign, have performed service beyond their station, continue to carry out their respective duties until the end of their protection. (7.201)

Even when such favor is being shown, if he should think that because of his subjects'— whether of the city or the countryside— or others' affection for him as their lord, he is highly esteemed due to his nature as a speaker and his majesty, and thus my own rod of punishment would be unable to prevail, then,
having understood the intentions of all these people in brief,
he should install one of their own lineage there and establish a formal covenant. (7.202)

Having understood in brief that this is the intention of the citizens and others—"He does not desire this; he wishes to make one born of that family [his successor]"—he should, in that very region, enter into an agreement with a member of that lineage who is mild, pure, and has a beloved and happy wife, together with his assembled subjects and principal officers, such as: "There shall be an equal distribution of treasury and gifts according to measure; you must act with me as if by divine decree, even if I am wicked; regarding what should and should not be done, you must present yourself personally at the proper time; and there shall be punishment from both sides, through both military force and the treasury," and so forth. (7.202)
And one should establish for them the righteous laws as they have been declared;
and one should honor him with jewels, together with the principal men.

Whatever types of established conditions they may have—whether previously acquired or long-standing, such as grants made by Brahmans, the livelihood of gods, or the management of temple property—the king should recognize and validate them as authoritative; for in this way, they will remain loyal to him. Furthermore, he should honor those who are the leading men there—with gifts of weapons, wealth, grain, ornaments, vehicles, umbrellas, thrones, and the binding of the royal fillet—on account of their promises, their large number of kinsmen, and other such qualities. (7.203)
But why, then, is the giving of jewels and such things from one's own possessions [recommended]? It is said:
Taking away is a cause of displeasure, whereas giving is a cause of pleasure;
therefore, the timely bestowal of desired objects is praised. (7.204)

The failure to bestow what is worthy of being accepted—whether by a new king or another—is an act that causes displeasure and is the cause of dissatisfaction. Conversely, giving and returning a gift are acts that produce pleasure; although both are well known to be so in many instances, when performed [at the right time], they bring about the desired objects and happiness, whereas otherwise they cause suffering—this is the meaning. That which is joined with the proper time and occurs at the opportune moment is praised; for even if something produces pleasure at a certain time, it does not produce pleasure if it is meager or unseemly. Therefore, one should perform the acts of giving and receiving in consideration of the proper time. (7.204)
Whatever has passed and whatever is yet to be told—
all this action is dependent upon the divine and the human.
Of these two, the divine is indeed inconceivable, whereas in the human there exists effort.

By implication, "action" here refers to the fruit that is the effect of an action. All of that, without exception, is dependent—that is, subject—to something. It is called a "disposer" (*vidhāna*) because it ordains; it is that which assigns the fruit of action. He specifies this as being twofold: divine (*daiva*) and human (*mānuṣa*). The divine refers to the fruit of one's own actions regarding dharma and so forth, within the scope of what was previously performed as prescribed or prohibited. If the fruit is the performance of action for a visible purpose, it pertains to right and wrong conduct. And thus says the Śruti:
"Disposer (*vidhi*), ordinance (*vidhāna*), necessity (*niyati*), inherent nature (*svabhāva*), time (*kāla*), Brahmā, Īśvara, action (*karma*), and fate (*daiva*)."
Fortune, merit, the inner conjunction of beings, and destiny are synonyms for what was done in a previous life; this is also confirmed by Smṛti:
"One should know that destiny is produced by oneself, like karma belonging to a former body."
"But human effort is said to be that which is performed here as something else."

Regarding the phrase "of the divine and the human," although it might have been understood [as referring only to the divine], by virtue of the context of death, the causality of the human is also intended. In this matter, this result of action depends upon that. Destiny does not bestow a fruit when devoid of human effort; for it must necessarily depend upon human exertion. Nor is human effort [dependent] upon destiny. Furthermore, from destiny alone, independent of human effort, there might even be the union of a person with a fruit—that is, a conception—even if no embryo exists; yet, in the absence of an embryo, the production of a fruit through the conjunction of destiny must be inferred [as impossible]. Likewise, if [the result] were independent of destiny even from human exertion, then it would always occur for everyone whenever there is physical effort. But this is not the case. Therefore, both are causes. And thus Vyāsa said:
"All human undertakings have their basis in two types of action:

destiny (*daiva*) and human effort (*puruṣakāra*); beyond these two, nothing else is found. (MBh 10.2.2). Also, in the *Samānatantra*: "Destiny [governs] right and wrong policy, while human action protects the world. (cf. KAŚ 6.2.6–7).

In this regard, the proponents of destiny (*daiva*) say: "Destiny alone is the cause here. For we observe that those who are dull-witted, impotent, lame, and the like—even those lacking human effort (*puruṣakāra*), being helpless and receiving the fruits of karma conditioned by other factors—are happy. Likewise, even those who are capable of counteracting [misfortune], who are unimpaired, heroic, proficient in the sciences, and skillful, are suffering despite their efforts. Furthermore, they perceive that desirable and undesirable results are produced through the mere influence of destiny, independent of human effort, such as the acquisition of wealth or the falling of a thunderbolt. And by accepting this, the instructions for undertaking actions that have the next world as their goal become all the more meaningful. Thus, knowing that 'we enjoy here the fruits of what was done previously with effort, and we shall enjoy in the next world what is done here,' humans remain free from doubt. One must strive in this way toward *dharma*. As they illustrate:"
I know the Dharma, yet I do not perform it;
I do not know evil, nor does it proceed from me. I am released by the Creator exactly as he has ordained.
"There is no one else who can command beyond this.

For those who act with human effort say: "In this world, human effort alone is the cause. One who is diligent in agriculture and performs his own task will obtain the fruit of his activity—the result of the agent, the instrument, and the action—such as farming and so forth. And thus it has been said:
"In this world, for those who are not wicked, it is karma alone that is to be relied upon and cultivated."
For having performed an action, a person experiences its result; he does not consume it, nor does he eat it.

Moreover, even when food is available, those who do not eat are not satisfied. In that case, the principle is that the fruit which arises immediately following the act of consumption is produced by means of that [act]. Therefore, in this instance, there is an invisible operation (*adṛṣṭavyāpāra*). And by establishing it thus, the instructions for undertaking ritual actions become purposeful. As they have said: "The Sage strikes down destiny whenever it has befallen him;
likewise, he brings forth cold, heat, and rain, and he destroys them."

When both [factors] are present, they serve as causes, for in the absence of either one, the fruit does not arise. However, in some cases, certain factors operate with predominance, and thus that [predominant factor] is what is grasped. Even human effort, once performed, is shattered when overcome by powerful destiny (*daiva*), just as wet wood thrown into a small fire does not blaze. Likewise, if weak destiny is preceded by great effort and human exertion, it bears fruit—just as even wet wood, when thrown into a great mass of fire, [is consumed]. In that case, the fire does not fail to reach it.
Indeed, destiny that is weak is overcome by human effort;
but intentional action is overcome by a superior destiny.
Having thus reflected, he said:

Between those two—destiny (*daiva*) and human effort (*puruṣakāra*)—destiny alone is inconceivable. The word *tu* (but) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Its essential nature is unknown; it is inconceivable in the sense that one cannot know at what time it will yield its fruit by means of that cause. Furthermore, apart from the scriptures, because its nature cannot be fully understood, and because it cannot be deliberated upon, it is impossible to employ; thus it is said to be "infeasible. In that regard, destiny is fruitless [as a controllable factor]. Among humans, human effort (*puruṣakāra*) will be explained as action (*kriyā*), since it is the subject under discussion. Wealth (*vitta*) and action belong to the human sphere. Some knowledge regarding agriculture and so forth can be conceived: "Such agriculture and so forth must be performed by me with these means, such as [the right season] and destiny, and its fruit will be such-and-such. Thus, when an undertaking has begun, if one desires to persist until the completion of that undertaking, then destiny should be reconciled [with one's efforts], thinking: "Even for those who have failed, this is how it should be done. Until the experience of the fruit, because destiny is inconceivable, one should not remain intent on it alone. Having reflected upon human action, whatever task is to be done should be performed. For he who acts haphazardly perishes.
An expedition endowed with both divine and human factors accomplishes all goals;
in such an undertaking, the divine factor prevails in its excellence, while the human factor remains equal.

When one who is endowed with the three powers and joined with human effort (*puruṣakāra*) desires the conquest of a foreign kingdom, that very desire becomes the accomplisher of all goals provided it is perfected by both fate (*daiva*) and human means. Nevertheless, in such a case, fate exerts its influence to a superior degree; the meaning is that human effort alone becomes excessive. For without the favor of fate for the conqueror, there occurs at that time the misfortune of the enemy, which consists of both fate and human factors. When human effort is equal to fate, it is not overly deployed; or when the two are equal, they are balanced. (7.205-a)
Moreover:
"Whatever human activity proceeds according to the decree of fate, it accomplishes its purpose only through great hardship. (7.205b)

That is improper; for when fate and human effort are turned away, personal exertion (*puruṣakāra*) proceeds toward the eightfold action, yet it achieves its purpose and fruit only with great hardship, or it becomes fruitless. Therefore, one should not be satisfied even if success is not achieved despite hardship, but rather remain dependent upon fate. (7.205-b)
But that human effort which proceeds when joined with destiny accomplishes all the purposes of counsel without difficulty. (7.205-c)

Human effort (*puruṣakāra*) is that which serves the human purpose. When that very effort is applied toward a destiny (*daiva*) that is exceedingly favorable, it becomes a means for accomplishing the complete fruit without difficulty and with absolute certainty. (7.205-c)
To confirm this point, there is an illustration in two verses:
"Some hold that even battle is a field [of action] joined with human effort, yet it yields fruit for someone who is devoid of destiny. (7.205d)
Some say that the field is "nourished" by human effort. (7.205-e)

Furthermore, when [the teaching] has been seen again and again, purified, and correctly explained, it does not yield its fruit for one who is devoid of the divine [factor], characterized by such benefits. || 7.205-d-e ||
Even when joined with destiny, if it is devoid of human effort, the field yields fruit without human effort. (7.205-f)

"Even for one who is joined [with effort], it is due to destiny (*daiva*). The conjunction with destiny, moreover, is inferred from that very granting of the fruit. And thus, the absence of that [effort] previously mentioned is the state of destiny. Others, however, say: "Destiny is that which, being sufficient at the proper time, is considered 'done' simply because of the perception of visible results and so forth; since it has been accomplished, it is as if it were already done. In this way, it demonstrates the absence of human effort (*puruṣakāra*), just as the phrase "devoid of seed" indicates the absence of a seed. (7.205-f)
The moon, the sun, and other planets, as well as wind, fire, and water—these are accomplished here through divine power and through human effort. (7.205-g)

The planets, beginning with the moon and the sun, are brought about by destiny—known as the inherent merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) of men—as the cause for the experience of pleasure and pain. When they reach undesirable positions, they are brought to equilibrium through human effort (*pauruṣa*) by means of methods such as propitiatory rites (*śānti*). Once established here in their proper places, they are made to act in accordance with non-deviation. (7.205-g)
Or, being prepared, he may even march together with him after carefully concluding a treaty, perceiving the threefold fruit consisting of allies, gold, or land. (7.206)

Having carefully considered the rear-attacker (*pārṣṇigrāha*) as well as the ally-in-distress (*ākranda*) within the circle of states, one should obtain the fruit of the expedition from either a friend or even an enemy. (7.207)
A king does not prosper so much by the acquisition of gold and land as he does by gaining a firm friend who, though currently weak, is capable of future success. (7.208)
One who knows the dharma, is grateful, and is naturally contented;
one who is devoted, steadfast in his undertakings—such a light friend is highly praised. (7.209)
The wise say it is a hardship to have for an enemy one who is intelligent, of noble birth, brave, skillful, generous, grateful, and steadfast. (7.210)
Nobility, knowledge of men, heroism, and a compassionate nature; constant magnanimity and the arising of the qualities of one who remains impartial—these are his traits. (7.211)

Knowledge of persons is knowledge of the world. One who knows the distinctions among persons provides assistance in a manner suited to them; he follows along, is heroic, and becomes capable of action. Through the pride of the quality of compassion, he perceives suffering and protects with a compassionate mind. Being of liberal nature (*sthūlalakṣa*), he at all times endures even great demands from these [persons]. (7.211)
A king should, without hesitation, abandon even land that is secure, always productive of crops, and conducive to the increase of cattle, for his own sake. (7.212)

One should abandon even such a territory without delay, provided it is secure and not subject to conquest by forest tribes (*āṭavika*) and the like. For him, both [types of territory] are always primary: that which has abundant crops and fertile soil, and that which promotes the increase of livestock due to its arid nature (*jāṅgala*), yet possesses plenty of fruit, leaves, and grass. Indeed, land with such qualities abounds in merchants and farmers, is free from famine and disease, and can sustain the inhabitants of the wilderness. In the fourth case, regarding the abandonment of the constituent elements (*prakṛti*), there is a dual consideration. One should not abandon the constituent elements of arms (*āyudha-prakṛti*) in that situation without first making them aware; rather, one should abandon that [territory] which one considers possible to recover later through the other constituent elements. However, just as there is no difference in the abandonment of allies, treasury, and army, one should abandon even a territory of excellent quality at every moment when one considers it so. (7.212)
One should save wealth for times of misfortune, and protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth;
one should always protect oneself, even at the cost of both wife and wealth. (7.213)

This rule is one that must be accomplished through arduous means; it is for the sake of an emergency (*āpad*). Just as smoke is known to be for the sake of mosquitoes—to drive away mosquitoes—one should protect wealth for that purpose alone; there is no other purpose for the protection of wealth. For wealth is that which has already yielded its fruit through being given or enjoyed. Thus, by means of it, he maintains vehicles, seats, and staffs, and wins over those who can be instigated. Even wives are to be protected by means of wealth. The mention of "wives" is intended to include messengers and kinsmen by marriage as well. However, the self (*ātman*) must be protected. If one is unable to protect oneself by any other means, one should give away all one's possessions and, even at the cost of abandoning one's wife at the proper time, remain restrained in speech and perform *dharma*, setting aside wife, wealth, and the like. As for those who perish out of attachment to wealth and wife, neither their wealth nor their wife serves any visible purpose, nor does it serve any invisible purpose, because they fail to practice *dharma* and *adharma*. Nor is there any abandonment of a wife from childhood (*kaumāradāratyāgitva*). This is not a prohibition against such abandonment. Furthermore, since this has been stated in the section on the duties of kings (*rājadharmaprakaraṇa*), it should be understood to apply to others as well, because its purpose is visible.

"But surely, once a king has obtained his kingdom and possesses great wealth, he will perform the horse sacrifice and other rites, and he will enjoy incomparable happiness; therefore, what can the world do to cause him distress? This is not a valid objection. For there are purifying acts even for one with little means, and practices such as the recitation of prayers (*japa*) even for one who is destitute. Wealth is merely a specific instrumental cause [for certain acts]. Furthermore, it is not the case that in this state [of poverty] the world's censure applies. Nor should this [ascetic life] be undertaken impulsively. (7.213)
For it is said: "Having carefully observed that all calamities arise together, a wise man should employ every means, both those already combined and those yet to be applied. (7.214)

"Calamities" (*āpadaḥ*) are misfortunes caused by divine or human agents; these, occurring simultaneously within the realm of the constituent elements (*prakṛti*), however excessively they may arise—so that they might be [overcome], a wise man should employ all means: conciliation preceded by gifts, sowing dissension preceded by conciliation, conciliation accompanied by gifts and dissension, or indeed force alone, or gift alone, and so forth. The meaning is that he should apply whatever is appropriate after having observed and deliberated upon it; he should not remain despondent. (7.214)
In response to the question "How so?", he says:
"Relying upon these three—the one who approaches, that which is to be approached, and all means in their entirety—one should strive for the accomplishment of the goal. (7.215)

There is an alternative reading: *sādhayet kāryam ātmanaḥ*. In that case, having approached the self as the seeker (*upetāram*), one should accomplish the task like a friend. All means (*sarvopāyāḥ*) are both collective (*samastāḥ*) and individual (*vyastāḥ*). This also provides a general indication of the goal (*upeya*). Having relied upon (*samāśritya*) and accepted [the means], this becomes encompassed by the consideration of their efficacy. For what purpose are the means approved by the capable? One should deliberate: "Is the capable person thus suitable? and "By which means among these might he obtain this? The term *kṛtsnaśaḥ* is a qualifier of the triad; its meaning is "entirely. Thus, whatever is to be accomplished by a particular means, whenever and however it is appropriate, one should employ that means at that time and in that manner for the sake of accomplishing every task. Since these states are infinite, it is impossible to state everything in detail within this treatise (*tantra*); therefore, it has been stated in brief. Consequently, one should apply critical examination (*parīkṣā*). He also speaks from the perspective of specific conditions (*viśeṣabhāvataḥ*) after having approached [the subject].
"For he who is disciplined indeed achieves his goal; one who is disciplined possesses personal prowess.
Both of these are endowed with statesmanship: even a thief when possessed of iron [a sword]. (7.215)
[336] Having thus deliberated on all this with his ministers, the king,
having exercised himself and bathed at midday, should enter the inner apartments to eat.

Thus, having deliberated with his ministers on all this conduct as it has been described—whether in times of calamity or not, or according to his own capacity, considering what ought to be done in each particular situation—the king, at the stated time of midday, having performed physical exercise and the prescribed bathing ritual; although bathing was mentioned out of sequence, it is stated again for the sake of the kingdom, as it is appropriate for those engaged in auspicious conduct. The concluding summary is that, for the purpose of undertaking the bath, the king should first go to the inner apartments (antaḥpura) which are provided with food and other necessities, rather than [going directly to] the bath itself. [This is] in a secluded place. (7.216)

There, having thoroughly examined the food and other edibles with attendants who are like his own self, who know the proper time, and who cannot be led astray, he should eat it while reciting mantras that counteract poison.

In that regard, within the inner apartments, he should eat all food and drink that has been examined by those who serve as his personal protectors—those who are like himself, who know the proper time (knowing the specific times determined by age, state, and so forth, for the giving of various kinds of food), who are unassailable, indivisible, and trustworthy, and who are attendants such as physicians and the like. The examination should be performed by skilled physicians using the *agnicakra* and other methods. When food is contaminated with poison, if it is dry, it becomes impure; there is discoloration and a loss of its natural fragrance. When thrown into the fire, it becomes excessively withered, or it emits a "ve-ti-ve-ti" sound, or the flames themselves become discolored. Furthermore, when observed, it causes the death of birds: where the cuckoo dies upon seeing it, the *jīvañjīvaka* bird withers, and the eyes of the *cakora* bird perish even when merely shown the poison; or there may be a contraction of the testicles, perspiration, and so forth. One should also recite over such things mantras that remove poison, especially against those who cause harm. (7.217)
He should mix all his substances with water that destroys poison, and, being self-restrained, he should always wear gems that counteract poison. (7.218)

With anti-poisonous waters, he should purify all the king's articles of use, such as garments and the like. [He should also employ] anti-poisonous gems, such as the *garuḍodīrṇa* and the *nāgadamaṇi*. He should always wear them at fixed times, both during mealtime and at other occasions. (7.218)
And women who have been thoroughly examined, purified by their dress and ornaments, and composed in mind, should touch him with fans, water, and incense. (7.219)

Women—whether wives, female slaves, or attendants—who have been tested and scrutinized through their integrity, purity, and conduct, may touch or serve [the king] by means of fans, water, and incense; they may do so while dressed in fine attire, having bathed and assumed various guises. Being composed, with undistracted minds, they may examine his ornaments and finery—his deceptive dress, hair, nails, and so forth. Perhaps, having placed weapons there, they might kill him with confidence; or they might touch him with ornaments smeared with poison. (7.219)
One should exert effort in this manner regarding vehicles, beds, seats, and food, as well as in bathing, grooming, and all forms of personal adornment. (7.220)

In this manner, one should exert effort regarding water for the feet, water for rinsing the mouth, gold, and so forth. "Bathing" refers to bathing the head; "fragrance" refers to yellow pigment (rocanā) and the like. "The seat" is mentioned here for the sake of illustration; for just as great care is exercised when seated there [on a seat], so too should it be exercised regarding vehicles and other such things. (7.220)
Having eaten, he should indeed enjoy himself with the women in the inner apartments;
but having enjoyed himself at the proper time, he should again attend to his duties. (7.221)

In that very inner apartment, for his own diversion, he should sport at ease with women, such as his newly-wedded wife and others. The phrase "at the proper time" is to be connected with the subsequent clause "as long as it is the time for recreation. Having enjoyed himself and being rested, he should again deliberate alone or with his ministers on the affairs that have arisen at the appropriate time. (7.221)
And having adorned himself, he should inspect the armed men again, as well as all the mounts, weapons, and ornaments. (7.222)

Having emerged from the inner apartments, adorned with ornaments, he should inspect the armed forces and grant them an audience. Because of the repetition of the word "again," even those who have been inspected in the forenoon must be seen daily. Effort should be made regarding the weapons and other equipment of those who live by arms, as well as all the mounts. Inspection of these is for the purpose of ascertaining their condition and for ensuring that those appointed to them apply special care to them. Therefore, the inspection of the staff and the livelihood of the dependents should be performed frequently at both times [morning and evening]. (7.222)
Having performed the twilight devotions, he should remain within his inner apartments bearing arms and listen to the reports of those who convey secrets and the activities of his spies. (7.223)

Although the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) has already been prescribed for the three *varṇas*, it is mentioned here again so that the duties regarding progeny might be postponed for some time, or for the sake of immediate sequence to the subsequent activities. "In the inner apartments" means in a secluded place such as a palace and so forth; "of those who report" refers to certain citizens or secret agents who have been recruited, and their conduct—conduct meaning their behavior—is what is intended. One should observe them at this time to determine what they have seen, heard, or done. This is for the purpose of not being discovered by others, and so that one who is composed may proceed with the timing of affairs as they arise according to the fixed schedule.

And just as one should observe the task once it has been undertaken so as not to cause distress, for [otherwise] it becomes difficult to accomplish or even impossible to achieve once it has passed its time. (7.223)
Having gone to another chamber and dismissed those people,
he should enter the inner apartments again, surrounded by women, for the purpose of eating.
Therefore, having gone from the house to another chamber and having dismissed that confidant who revealed the secret, he should re-enter the inner apartments surrounded by women attendants. 7.224.
Having eaten there once more a little, gladdened by the sounds of musical instruments, he should go to rest at the proper time and rise with his fatigue dispelled. (7.225)

The word *kiṃcit* is an indeclinable. *Tūryāṇi* refers to musical instruments such as the flute, lute, cymbals, drum, kettle-drum, conch, and so forth. Delighted by their gentle sounds, which are pleasing to the ear, one should go to bed at the proper time—that is, one should pass that time which is appropriate for sleep. Having dispelled fatigue and being free from all suffering, one should rise to attend to one's duties. (7.225)
A healthy lord of the earth should observe this rule;
but when he is unwell, he should entrust all of this to his servants. (7.226)

Regarding this which was previously mentioned—"at midday or at midnight" (MDh 7.151)—his conduct and activity should be such that he personally attends to it; he should station himself there and assign [tasks] to his servants, meaning he should employ them. He should do so for as long as he is able. Thus, having arranged for the activities of self-protection through independent agents, he accomplishes the business of both his subjects and himself. (7.226)
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Duties of Kings," in the Saṃhitā of Manu’s Dharmaśāstra as proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the Commentary on Manu, composed by Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi, son of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Vīrasvāmin.
